title: titleRequest 3974
summary: In committing to the realization of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, Member States recognized that the dignity of the individuals is fundamental and that the Agendaâ€™s Goals and targets should be met for all nations and people and for all segments of society. Ensuring that these commitments are translated into effective action requires a precise understanding of the target populations and progress made in addressing their particular priorities.  / To properly measure this, statistics need to be presented for different population groups and geographical areas. The Global Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator framework has included an overarching principle of data disaggregation: Sustainable Development Goal indicators should be disaggregated, where relevant, by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability and geographic location, or other characteristics, in accordance with the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics.  / Small area estimation (SAE) techniques have been proved to be very useful to provide reliable disaggregated data for some SDG indicators, such as poverty estimation, food insecurity and undernutrition, health related indicators, unemployment rate, etc.   / Under the guidance of IAEG-SDGs and ISWGHS, a draft set of Toolkit has been developed by UNSD on small area estimation for SDGs.  The Toolkit provides guidance to countries, based on national experiences, on the use of small area estimation for SDG data disaggregation.  The Toolkit covers essential elements of the use of small area estimation including the use of input data, modelling, data validation and dissemination. The Toolkit also provides practical guidance to countries on how to move from SAE experiments to official production.   / In this regard, the UN Statistics Division (as the secretariat of both the Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Household Surveys and IAEG-SDGs working on SAE) is (a) fianlising the SAE Toolkit for SDG data disaggregation; and (b) developing a set of eLearning courses on small area estimation for SDGs data disaggregation, in collaboration with ECLAC Statistics Division and UNFPA .

title: titleFSDO will organize two 2-day regional workshops on strengthening the capacity of developing countries to design risk-informed and data driven development cooperation strategies and policies in support of their COVID-19 response and recovery efforts. In addition, demand for peer learning and capacity building activities has been repeatedly expressed by government representatives in DCF policy dialogue (e.g., 2021 DCF High-level Meeting of ECOSOC; DCF regional consultations in December 2021).    / In the Outcome document of the 2022 Financing for Development (FfD) Forum, Member States highlighted â€œthe critical role of resilient international development cooperation in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and addressing global crises, as highlighted by the 2021 high-level meeting of the Development Cooperation Forum.â€ Moreover, they committed â€œto support developing countries in strengthening their capacities at the national and local levels to manage and reduce risks, which entails developing institutional capacities for transitioning to resilient and sustainable development systems.â€  / Based on the above mandates, FSDO and on exchanges with 2021/2022 DCF Survey participants from the Africa and Asia-Pacific regions, FSDO plans to offer the two workshops, which will result in improved knowledge and understanding to advance risk-informed development cooperation for long term resilience, as well as strengthen data systems for monitoring and evaluation for effective development cooperation. / Original reference# 4221

title: titlePresentations at the Asia-Pacific Regional Virtual Meeting on Using National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for Intergenerational Policy Advancement, 5-6 October, Jakarta, Indonesia / This virtual meeting sponsored by UNFPA was attended by 155 NTA practitioners, academicians, and government officials from 20 countries in the Asia-Pacific region to discuss the use of evidence from National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for developing forward-looking, intergenerational policies to meet the challenges and opportunities brought about by rapid population change in the region.  I served as panelist on a roundtable discussion on "Improving National Transfer Accounts as a Policy Tool" and also gave a presentation on DESA's Handbook on Population Ageing and Sustainable Development -- which examines issues of intergenerational equity, economic security, fiscal sustainability, and sustainable economic growth. / Presentation at the Asia-Pacific Regional Virtual Meeting on Using National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for Ageing Policy Advancement, 7 October, Jakarta, Indonesia / This virtual meeting sponsored by UNFPA was attended by 60 policy planners and government officials from 20 countries in the Asia-Pacific region to receive feedback on the usefulness of National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for national planning in response to population ageing. summary: The request is based on an overall demand from National Statistical Systems (NSS) overall in developing countries for support in producing more timely and disaggregated SDG indicators as well as information on COVID-19 using administrative data for statistical purposes. As a response to this, the Collaborative on Administrative Data was established in June 2020. It was presented to the UN Statistical Commission in March 2021, also based on earlier requests from the Commission in earlier years and through the Inter-Agency Expert Group on SDGs (IAEG-SDG). It received strong endorsement and support from the UN Statistical Commission in 2021. / Overall, there is a strong need to increase the knowledge on how to better make use of administrative data for statistics production in countries.. If such data sources are of sufficient quality, they reduce response burden on the population, reduce data collection costs and they may give a more complete and disaggregated picture of a situation than other sources. Many countries are, however, still struggling to use this source of data and through the Collaborative (and before that through a number of other channels), they have expressed a strong need for capacity development and training support. As part of the Collaborative, there has been much work, led by the countries that are members of the Collaborative, to collect currently available guidance, and where lacking, specifying needs for additional practical tools and guidance materials. As members, including international partners, have limited capacity to respond to these requests for practical guidance tools, it is, among others, proposed to hire consultant(s) who can support the work and help it progress more quickly. That way, countries will also be able to increase their efforts to provide more timely and disaggregated information on the SDGs and COVID-19 / This has mainly taken place through informal online meetings orally with no formal meeting minutes and cant therefore be attached as files to this request.   / An overview of the Collaborative and the task teams can be found here: https://unstats.un.org/capacity-development/admin-data/

title: titleThe mandate for the proposed activity comes from the resolution adopted by the 56th session of the United Nations Statistical Commission (to be adopted by Economic and Social Council later in 2025) on the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme as well as decision 56/102 of the Statistical Commission. Both the resolution and the decision recognize censuses as key for formulating, implementing, and monitoring inclusive socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability policies, and as a vital source of disaggregated data for tracking the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, including assessments by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location, and other characteristics. As part of the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme, which includes several inter-related objectives and activities, UNSD is mandated to develop international statistical standards, methods, and guidelines to facilitate the conduct of population and housing censuses, and to provide technical assistance for building national capacity in planning and conducting censuses.
summary: The request is for a capacity building workshop to prepare census managers in Asian countries to successfully plan their 2030 round censuses and to effectively implement the Revision 4 of the United Nations Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (P&R Rev.4), endorsed by the 56th session of the Statistical Commission in March 2025. summary: The System of Environmental Economic Accounting (SEEA) provides the internationally agreed statistical framework for measuring the relationship between the environment and the economy. It is comprised of two complimentary international statistical standards: the SEEA Central Framework (SEEA CF) and the SEEA Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA). The SEEA can be flexibly implemented by countries prioritizing accounts based on availability of information and policy priorities. The accounts are designed to respond to data needs for multiple policy initiatives including global initiatives on sustainable development goals (SDGs), on mitigating and adapting to climate change, disaster related statistics and on measuring the contribution of the environment to well-being. The accounts are also a necessary input to the compilation of headline indicators such as net domestic product as part of the recently adopted 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA). / In Asia, good progress has been made in the compilation of SEEA accounts with many countries regularly compiling SEEA CF accounts. National statistical offices (NSOs) of countries in the region continue to express strong interest in compiling SEEA accounts, including taking steps towards compiling asset accounts which are relevant for informing the relationship between the economy and the environment. With the recent adoption of the 2025 SNA which has expanded its asset boundary to include several natural resources assets of the SEEA CF, demands for environmental asset accounts will increase as the SEEA CF can provide input data for the compilation of the 2025 SNA. More broadly, there is a need to strengthen the capacities of NSOs to produce and disseminate SEEA accounts to better meet the needs of users for high quality integrated data on the contribution of the environment to the economy and the impact of the economy on the environment.

title: titleStatistical training is key to increasing the skills of staff at National Statistical Offices (NSOs) and the wider National Statistical System (NSS). In many low- and middle-income countries, there is, however, no systematic institutional plan in place to ensure the capacity development of staff. The Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) has developed the Statistical Training needs Assessment Tool (STAT) which the NSO can use to identify, prioritize, and meet training needs among staff and within the NSS. Before STAT was launched at the 55th UNSC, STAT was piloted in six countries with two countries (Ghana and Colombia) participating in a more thorough pilot. STAT is still a very new tool with a need to continue testing and thus learning from those countries who in this early phase decide to implement STAT. This includes among others learning more about the phase of developing an institutional training plan, how to implement it, and how to increase the use of e-learning and other non-classroom-based training.
summary: Following the presentation of STAT (see notes above) at the UN Statistical Commission in 2024, a number of countries have contacted UNSD and other GIST members as they want to implement STAT in their countries (all those listed in this demand proposal). Several of these do need support to implement STAT. Other GIST members are looking at supporting some of the countries, and UNSD is hoping to support a selected number of African countries that have requested the support. Attached are a few requests that have been formalized in writing.

title: titleRequest 3974
summary: In committing to the realization of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, Member States recognized that the dignity of the individuals is fundamental and that the Agendaâ€™s Goals and targets should be met for all nations and people and for all segments of society. Ensuring that these commitments are translated into effective action requires a precise understanding of the target populations and progress made in addressing their particular priorities.  / To properly measure this, statistics need to be presented for different population groups and geographical areas. The Global Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator framework has included an overarching principle of data disaggregation: Sustainable Development Goal indicators should be disaggregated, where relevant, by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability and geographic location, or other characteristics, in accordance with the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics.  / Small area estimation (SAE) techniques have been proved to be very useful to provide reliable disaggregated data for some SDG indicators, such as poverty estimation, food insecurity and undernutrition, health related indicators, unemployment rate, etc.   / Under the guidance of IAEG-SDGs and ISWGHS, a draft set of Toolkit has been developed by UNSD on small area estimation for SDGs.  The Toolkit provides guidance to countries, based on national experiences, on the use of small area estimation for SDG data disaggregation.  The Toolkit covers essential elements of the use of small area estimation including the use of input data, modelling, data validation and dissemination. The Toolkit also provides practical guidance to countries on how to move from SAE experiments to official production.   / In this regard, the UN Statistics Division (as the secretariat of both the Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Household Surveys and IAEG-SDGs working on SAE) is (a) fianlising the SAE Toolkit for SDG data disaggregation; and (b) developing a set of eLearning courses on small area estimation for SDGs data disaggregation, in collaboration with ECLAC Statistics Division and UNFPA .

title: titlePresentations at the Asia-Pacific Regional Virtual Meeting on Using National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for Intergenerational Policy Advancement, 5-6 October, Jakarta, Indonesia / This virtual meeting sponsored by UNFPA was attended by 155 NTA practitioners, academicians, and government officials from 20 countries in the Asia-Pacific region to discuss the use of evidence from National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for developing forward-looking, intergenerational policies to meet the challenges and opportunities brought about by rapid population change in the region. Following the roundtable,  a staff member of UNFPA and I discussed the UN's past contributions and future support on the use of National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for policy development in the Asia-Pacific region.

title: titleFSDO will carry out research into the digitalization of tax administration processes in response to a request by the Iranian National Tax Administration (INTA) (letter from INTA to FSDO is attached in this demand repository). Iran is interested to see how other countries have gone about the process of digitalizing revenue administration processes with a view to learning from the experiences and best practices towards establishing a â€˜smart tax systemâ€™.  / Digitalization of processes can be one of the most effective mechanisms to enhance revenue collection and enforcement, as it will improve efficiency and effectiveness of tax collection. These processes can play an important role in reducing risk and building resilience by strengthening developing countries tax enforcement and collection mechanisms to enhance revenue generation and administration, thereby supporting these countriesâ€™ domestic resource mobilization efforts for the achievement of the SDGs.  / FSDO has considered the request by INTA and finds that the research will be useful not only for Iran but for other developing countries in the midst of or considering digitalizing their tax administration processes. Moreover, the work will be beneficial for the UN Tax Committeeâ€™s small group on digitalization of tax processes, which is anticipated to inform future UN capacity development work in this area.  / Accordingly, the research would cover the following aspects from the digitalization of tax administrations perspective: (i) the definition of/criteria for determining a smart tax system; (ii) the role and position of different departments/units (such as information technology) within the tax administration in the process of digitalization; (iii) the role of other government departments in the digitalization process; and (iv) examples of countries that have successfully implemented smart tax systems.  / In the Outcome document of the 2022 Financing for Development (FfD) Forum, Member States recommitted to strengthening the capacities of revenue administration through modernized, transparent and progressive tax systems, improved tax policy and more efficient tax collection (E/FFDF/2022/L.1, p. 4.). To this end, Member States called upon the international community to scale up support for capacity-building to developing countries, especially in building their tax policy and administration capacities. In resolution 68/204 of 20 December 2013 (A/RES/68/204), the General Assembly recalled the commitment of Member States to enhance and strengthen domestic resource mobilization and fiscal space, including through modernized tax systems and the broadening of tax base. The same resolution reiterated the importance of supporting national efforts in these areas by strengthening technical assistance and enhancing international cooperation and participation in addressing international tax matters.  / In response to the request of the INTA, UNDESA commissioned a general research paper on relevant, specified aspects of the digitalization of tax administration processes. In June 2023, DESA shared the research paper with the Tax Administration, which introduces the subject and lays out key considerations for tax authorities in the journey to digitalizing their tax administrations. For reference, a short note from UNDESA was also sent to the INTA summarizing some aspects of the structure of the paper.
summary: The request was initiated by Iran, but it will help other developing countries understand specific aspects of the digitalization of tax administration processes to mitigate risk, build resilience and enforce revenue collection to finance the SDGs.

title: titlePresentations at the Asia-Pacific Regional Virtual Meeting on Using National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for Intergenerational Policy Advancement, 5-6 October, Jakarta, Indonesia / This virtual meeting sponsored by UNFPA was attended by 155 NTA practitioners, academicians, and government officials from 20 countries in the Asia-Pacific region to discuss the use of evidence from National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for developing forward-looking, intergenerational policies to meet the challenges and opportunities brought about by rapid population change in the region. summary: The request is based on an overall demand from National Statistical Systems (NSS) overall in developing countries for support in producing more timely and disaggregated SDG indicators as well as information on COVID-19 using administrative data for statistical purposes. As a response to this, the Collaborative on Administrative Data was established in June 2020. It was presented to the UN Statistical Commission in March 2021, also based on earlier requests from the Commission in earlier years and through the Inter-Agency Expert Group on SDGs (IAEG-SDG). It received strong endorsement and support from the UN Statistical Commission in 2021. / Overall, there is a strong need to increase the knowledge on how to better make use of administrative data for statistics production in countries.. If such data sources are of sufficient quality, they reduce response burden on the population, reduce data collection costs and they may give a more complete and disaggregated picture of a situation than other sources. Many countries are, however, still struggling to use this source of data and through the Collaborative (and before that through a number of other channels), they have expressed a strong need for capacity development and training support. As part of the Collaborative, there has been much work, led by the countries that are members of the Collaborative, to collect currently available guidance, and where lacking, specifying needs for additional practical tools and guidance materials. As members, including international partners, have limited capacity to respond to these requests for practical guidance tools, it is, among others, proposed to hire consultant(s) who can support the work and help it progress more quickly. That way, countries will also be able to increase their efforts to provide more timely and disaggregated information on the SDGs and COVID-19 / This has mainly taken place through informal online meetings orally with no formal meeting minutes and cant therefore be attached as files to this request.   / An overview of the Collaborative and the task teams can be found here: https://unstats.un.org/capacity-development/admin-data/

title: titleReport of 55th Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2024), decision 55/109 (h): / o	The Statistical Commission supported the efforts of international organizations, regional commissions and statistical training institutes in providing technical assistance, organizing workshops and training and developing compilation tools, and noted the importance of ensuring that resources continue to be made available for this work  / Report of the 50th Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2019), decision 50/115 (c): / o	The Statistical Commission requested the Committee of Experts to continue its work on mainstreaming the use of SEEA for policy processes, in particular with regards to biodiversity, in view of the adoption of the post-2020 biodiversity agenda, and climate change, circular economy, beyond gross domestic product (GDP) and green growth initiatives / Report of the 42nd Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2011), para. 105 (a), (b), (c): / o	The Statistical Commission welcomed with appreciation the report of the Secretary General on energy statistics (E/CN.3/2011/8) and noted that the work undertaken on the international recommendations for energy statistics illustrates effective cooperation among different agencies, expert groups and countries; adopted the international recommendations for energy statistics; endorsed the main elements of the proposed implementation programme
summary: Climate change is one of the most pressing policy issues around the world, with all countries being vulnerable to its adverse effects. To better mitigate climate change, countries are more and more looking to understand how to use energy more effectively and sustainably. Such an understanding requires countries to have high-quality energy statistics, balances and accounts. Together, energy statistics, balances and accounts can provide governments with the data they need to understand how the energy sector can be made more efficient and sustainable; how the economy can be made more energy efficient; and how changes in energy use can contribute to fewer emissions. ESCWA countries have expressed interest in capacity building on energy statistics and accounts. In addition, according to the 2023 Global Assessment on Environmental-Economic Accounting, Jordan plans to restart compilation of System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) accounts; Morocco and Tunisia have plans to expand its compilation of SEEA accounts; and Somalia has plans to begin compilation of SEEA accounts. / National statistical offices are well placed to produce energy statistics, balances and accounts. Energy statistics and balances can be compiled according to the International Recommendations for Energy Statistics (IRES), and energy accounts can be compiled according to the international statistical standard, the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA). At the same time, there is a need to strengthen the capacity of national statistical offices and other relevant ministries to produce and disseminate energy statistics, balances and accounts to better meet user needs.  / UNSD, in collaboration with ESCWA, SESRIC, IEA and AITRS held the workshop, "Energy Statistics, Balances and Accounts for Informed Energy and Climate Policies" from 10-12 December in Ankara. More than 40 participants from national statistical offices and ministries of energy came together from 10-12 December 2024 in Ankara to build capacity compilation and use of energy statistics, balances and accounts to support the dissemination of high-quality data for energy and climate change policies. The workshop also covered the institutional mechanisms needed to strengthen the institutions producing these statistics and allowed countries to share their experiences.

title: titleRequest 3989
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic presented a major challenge for household survey programmes. Traditional face-to-face survey operations have become difficult to implement in many countries due to social distancing requirements and other restriction measures as a result of the pandemic. According to a survey conducted by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD) and the World Bank in May 2020, 96â€¯percent of national statistical offices (NSOs) partially or fully stopped face-to-face data collection. / In response to the government requirement on social distancing, many national statistical offices (NSOs) quickly turned to telephone or web interviews as an alternative data collection mode to maintain continuity in the production of key indicators and monitor the health and socio-economic impact of the pandemic.    / In the fourth round of UNSD and the World Bank survey of national statistical offices in May-June 2021, a marked increase was observed in the number of countries declaring a full resumption of face-to-face data collection activities. Globally 44 percent of the surveyed countries resumed full face-to-face data collection, compared to just four percent a year earlier. / While the adaptation of national household survey operations indicated the resilience of NSOs, such adaptation also raised challenges for countries on survey data quality. Change of survey data collection mode from face-to-face to telephone or web may impact on sample coverage, response rate and measurement error. Shortening survey questionnaires and changing question flows will also impact on the quality and comparability of survey data.   / In close consultation with the Task Force on COVID-19, established by the Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Household Surveys (ISWGHS), UNSD is hiring a consultant to develop a Guidance Note on Assessing and Minimizing the COVID Impact on Survey Quality.

title: titleWhile the SDGs are global in nature, their achievement largely depends on local action. Local governments, communities, and individuals play a critical role in implementing and localising the SDGs by tailoring them to the specific context, needs, and priorities of their local areas. Three SDG indicators directly necessitate reporting of SDG indicators at the city level: SDG 11.2.1 , SDG 11.6.1 , and SDG 11.7.1 ; yet almost all indicators are relevant at the local city level, underscoring the importance and the localization agenda, at the global level too. In this regard, consistent standardized geographical names are a key resource for Member States as they are the â€˜glueâ€™ that helps bind data together. / In this regard, this workshop on â€œLinking Geographical Names, the Disaggregation and Localisation of SDGs, and the Semantic Webâ€ will take a deep dive into the importance of unique identifiers and toponyms for countries, cities, and geographic features as a means of integrating data for the SDGs. The workshop will examine the important role of both bottom-up and top-down toponymic metadata management to support efforts led by National Geospatial Names Authorities (NGNAs), National Geospatial Information Agencies (NGIAs), and other national actors responsible for geographical names and help promote the sharing of good practices between Member States. With the principle aim of developing national technical capacity in the area of geographical names standardization, participants will examine the characteristics of good linked open data infrastructure within their national context; developing a machine-readable, AI-ready gazetteers of their national data within CALIPER; and supporting its integration (and eventual federation) with the World Geographical Name Database, in accordance with UNGEGN mandates, principally, decision 2025/8.
summary: In accordance with Economic and Social Council resolution E/RES/2018/2 of 10 November 2017 and decision 2023/338 of 25 July 2023, the United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names convened its 2025 session from 28 April to the 2 May 2025 at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, in conference room three. There were 9 meetings of the 2025 session and each meeting will be three hours: 10:00 a.m - 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 - 6:00 p.m.. In all, 197 participants representing 56 Member States across UNGEGNâ€™s geographical and linguistic divisions and observers participated. Specifically, decision 2025/8 Geographical names data management (f): Urged Member States to mobilize resources to support the development of capacity across all Member States and welcomed the possibility of convening a workshop on Linking Geographical Names, the Disaggregation and Localization of Sustainable Development Goals, and the Semantic Web from 11 to 15 August 2025 at the headquarters of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean in Santiago.

title: titleThis proposal for technical assistance will be in response to a request from the Government of Jamaica, through the Executive Office of the Commissioner-General of the Tax Administration Jamaica, expressed in a letter of 30 January 2024 to the Acting Director of the Financing for Sustainable Development Office, Ms. Shari Spiegel. The Commissioner General then requested for Jamaica to be among a pilot program and received targeted technical assistance to identify and strengthen vulnerabilities in taxation policy and administration. title: titleThis proposal for a national workshop responds to the request from the Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) for technical assistance on tax dispute resolution (please see additional information in the â€œRequest summaryâ€, section below), including on the mutual agreement procedure (MAP), with the purpose of building the capacity of its staff dealing with international taxation issues from policy, audit and compliance perspectives.  / MAP is the tax dispute resolution procedure provided for in tax treaties. It plays a crucial role in promoting the fulfilment of treaty obligations and preventing obstacles to international trade and investment. It is particularly relevant for developing country policymakers and tax administrations because the fair and effective resolution of tax disputes supports an integrated approach to raising revenues and attracting and keeping foreign direct investment. This approach is critical to mobilizing and managing effectively the different forms of financing needed to implement the Addis Ababa Action Agenda (AAAA) and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

title: titleFSDO organized, in collaboration with the Caribbean Organisation of Tax Administrators (COTA), a 5-day regional workshop on the Practical Application of Mutual Agreement Procedure (MAP) from 5 to 9 December 2022. summary: The request is based on an overall demand from National Statistical Systems (NSS) overall in developing countries for support in producing more timely and disaggregated SDG indicators as well as information on COVID-19 using administrative data for statistical purposes. As a response to this, the Collaborative on Administrative Data was established in June 2020. It was presented to the UN Statistical Commission in March 2021, also based on earlier requests from the Commission in earlier years and through the Inter-Agency Expert Group on SDGs (IAEG-SDG). It received strong endorsement and support from the UN Statistical Commission in 2021. / Overall, there is a strong need to increase the knowledge on how to better make use of administrative data for statistics production in countries.. If such data sources are of sufficient quality, they reduce response burden on the population, reduce data collection costs and they may give a more complete and disaggregated picture of a situation than other sources. Many countries are, however, still struggling to use this source of data and through the Collaborative (and before that through a number of other channels), they have expressed a strong need for capacity development and training support. As part of the Collaborative, there has been much work, led by the countries that are members of the Collaborative, to collect currently available guidance, and where lacking, specifying needs for additional practical tools and guidance materials. As members, including international partners, have limited capacity to respond to these requests for practical guidance tools, it is, among others, proposed to hire consultant(s) who can support the work and help it progress more quickly. That way, countries will also be able to increase their efforts to provide more timely and disaggregated information on the SDGs and COVID-19 / This has mainly taken place through informal online meetings orally with no formal meeting minutes and cant therefore be attached as files to this request.   / An overview of the Collaborative and the task teams can be found here: https://unstats.un.org/capacity-development/admin-data/

title: titleFor more information, see https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/events/latin-america-and-caribbean-workshop-assessing-economic-and-fiscal-consequences-population. / This type of regional training workshop was first piloted at UN ESCAP.   Also note that ECLAC (Pop Division) undertook coordination of a project financed by the United Nations Development Account (10th Tranche) on Demographic Transition: Opportunities and Challenges to Achieve the SDGs in Latin America and the Caribbean.   Seminar was held immediately following this training workshop. / Achievement of an inclusive economic development that leaves no one behind requires good investment and good planning. Because achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030 also means ensuring their sustainability beyond 2030, training in the use of long-run population, economic, and fiscal forecasts is an important component of capacity development as envisioned by Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing.  /   / In this context, the Population Division of DESA and ECLAC organized the Latin American and Caribbean Workshop Assessing the Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Population Ageing, held at ECLAC in Santiago from 9 to 11 September 2019.  /   / While population ageing will be one of the most important forces shaping the outcome of social and economic policy in the coming decades in the Latin America and Caribbean region, it is not always explicitly included in policy discussions. Because its influence is difficult to discern in the short run, a myopic policy focus inevitably results in delays in addressing mounting challenges such as population ageing, climate change, non-communicable disease and environmental degradation.  /   / The Workshop trained participants from national statistical offices, ministries in the planning, economic and social sectors, and research institutions in the use medium- and long-run economic and fiscal forecasts to address the cost, equity, and sustainability of development policies and programmes.

titleUNSD has supported Member States in building capacity for SDMX-based reporting and dissemination, especially for MDGs and SDGs. This has led to the development of SDG dissemination platforms in several regions, funded mainly by extra-budgetary sources. RPTC has played a growing role, notably through a successful UNSD-ESCWA initiative in the Arab region. However, many developing countries still require advanced training to fully leverage SDMX.
summary: UNSD is preparing a use case to demonstrate the dissemination of data and the integration of SDG metadata into statistical outputs using the SDMX standard. This initiative focuses on linking SDG metadata with the UNdata mobile applications to enhance the accessibility and usability of statistical information. This use case can be used in workshops and guide participants through the process of extracting SDG data and metadata and integrating them into digital products. To support this, UNSD plans to update both UNdata Android and iOS apps with the latest available 2025 data - these updates will mirror the content of the printed Pocketbook publication. For each included SDG indicator, the apps will feature direct links to corresponding metadata, enabling users to explore definitions, methodologies, and sources seamlessly. / To ensure a fully functional and user-friendly experience, UNSD also plans to address several technical issues identified by both internal and external users in the SDG user interface, APIs and metadata related components of the system. This project not only enhances the visibility and utility of SDG data and metadata but also promotes best practices in data and metadata integration and digital dissemination using SDMX standards. / The proposal covers the contractual services needed to update the UNdata apps and fix some components in the SDG infrastructure, including SDG metadata.

title: titleRequest 5280
summary: UNSD conducts an annual Global Assessment of Environmental-Economic Accounting and Supporting Statistics (https://seea.un.org/content/global-assessment-environmental-economic-accounting) to monitor the implementation of the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) in countries. This assessment provides critical insights into global progress and challenges in integrating environmental and economic data and is the basis for the monitoring of SDG indicator 15.9.1(b). While the number of countries implementing the SEEA has steadily increased since 2014, recent assessments indicate that this growth has plateaued, suggesting that many countries may be encountering persistent barriers to further implementation. / This stagnation underscores the urgent need to strengthen national capacities for compiling SEEA accounts. Many countries, particularly those in the early stages of implementation, face challenges related to technical expertise, institutional coordination, data availability, and methodological understanding. Addressing these challenges requires targeted support and knowledge exchange. The proposed activity will facilitate peer learning and collaboration among countries. Through the sharing of practical experiences, lessons learned, and innovative approaches, countries will gain valuable insights into overcoming common obstacles and advancing their SEEA implementation. / Target countries will learn from the sharing of country experiences in the compilation of environmental accounts of other countries and how those countries have addressed challenges both in the implementation of the accounts and in the developments of concepts, methods and tools to address these challenges. / This activity also facilitates South-South cooperation, enabling countries with similar development contexts to support one another. It promotes mutual learning, strengthens regional and global networks, and builds lasting partnerships. The London Group meetings, which attract a wide range of countries at various stages of SEEA implementation as well as key international organizations, provide an ideal platform for such an engagement. These meetings facilitate dialogue, encourage innovation, and help align national efforts with global standards and best practices. By building capacity through collaboration and shared learning, it empowers countries to produce high-quality environmental-economic accounts that inform sustainable development policies and contribute to achieving the SDGs.

title: titleEndorsed by the United Nations Statistical Commission in June 2008, SDMX is recognized as a preferred standard for data and its related meta-information, and has been approved as an ISO standard (17369:2013). The SDMX initiative was started and is sponsored by eight international organizations (BIS, ECB, Eurostat, OECD, ILO, IMF, UN, and WB). / As coordinator of the Working Group on SDMX for SDG Indicators established by the IAEG-SDGs, UNSD has a responsibility for, and has delivered, capacity building to the Member States in SDMX for SDG monitoring. In different sessions, the UN Statistical Commission has stressed the need for continued technical and financial support for countries to build capacity for the production, monitoring, and reporting of Sustainable Development Goals indicators, including on SDMX and implementing the SDG Geospatial Roadmap. / The workshop is organized jointly by UN ESCWA and UNSD to improve countriesâ€™ skills in mapping, converting, and disseminating SDG data and metadata, raise awareness of the latest developments and promote the implementation of SDMX at the national level. / The workshop is planned to take place in Muscat, Oman, on 10-13 November 2025 (4 days).
summary: At  the 15th session of the ESCWA Statistical Committee, on 16-17 Nov 2022, the member States requested the ESCWA Secretariat to "Support member States in developing strategies to bridge gaps in data flows for sustainable, development indicators, so as to ensure the sustainability and modernization of national reporting platforms, and to exchange statistical data and metadata nationally between components of statistical systems using modern technologies, such as SDMX, to ensure that no one is left behindâ€¦â€ , which follows similar requests made at previous sessions.  / ESCWA and UNSD are addressing these through a series of joint online and in-person training events on SDMX-based dissemination and exchange of SDG data and metadata. The workshop in question is the 8th in the series and will directly contribute to the member Statesâ€™ capacity to exchange and disseminate SDG data and metadata using the global standards and advanced tools, and implementation of SDMX data exchange at the national level.  / The workshop is organized jointly by UN ESCWA and UNSD and is planned to take place in Muscat, Oman, on 10-13 November 2025 (4 days). A pre-workshop meeting will be held on 9 November 2025 to check the venue and final coordination for the event. The Workshop will bring together statisticians and IT specialists from various national statistical offices in the Arab region. / This workshop is a continuation of UNSD and ESCWAâ€™s work to improve and strengthen the SDMX skills of Member States on SDG data reporting and to implement SDMX at the national level. As requested by Member States in the region, the training will cover different SDMX topics and provide hands on exercises with the aim to introduce SDMX tools to enable the automation of data and metadata exchange between entities. It will employ a variety of tools including presentations, hands-on exercises, and the sharing of good practices and challenges by countries through discussions and presentations.

summary: Climate change is one of the most pressing policy issues around the world, with all countries being vulnerable to its adverse effects. Such an understanding requires countries to have high-quality energy statistics, balances and accounts. Together, energy statistics, balances and accounts can provide governments with the data they need to understand how the energy sector can be made more efficient and sustainable; how the economy can be made more energy efficient; and how changes in energy use can contribute to fewer emissions. ESCWA countries have expressed interest in capacity building on energy statistics and accounts. In addition, according to the 2023 Global Assessment on Environmental-Economic Accounting, Jordan plans to restart compilation of System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) accounts; Morocco and Tunisia have plans to expand its compilation of SEEA accounts; and Somalia has plans to begin compilation of SEEA accounts. / National statistical offices are well placed to produce energy statistics, balances and accounts. Energy statistics and balances can be compiled according to the International Recommendations for Energy Statistics (IRES), and energy accounts can be compiled according to the international statistical standard, the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA). At the same time, there is a need to strengthen the capacity of national statistical offices and other relevant ministries to produce and disseminate energy statistics, balances and accounts to better meet user needs.  / UNSD, in collaboration with ESCWA, SESRIC, IEA and AITRS held the workshop, "Energy Statistics, Balances and Accounts for Informed Energy and Climate Policies" from 10-12 December in Ankara. title: titleStatistical training is key to increasing the skills of staff at National Statistical Offices (NSOs) and the wider National Statistical System (NSS). This includes among others learning more about the phase of developing an institutional training plan, how to implement it, and how to increase the use of e-learning and other non-classroom-based training.

summary: The System of Environmental Economic Accounting (SEEA) provides the internationally agreed statistical framework for measuring the relationship between the environment and the economy. It is comprised of two complimentary international statistical standards: the SEEA Central Framework (SEEA CF) and the SEEA Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA). The SEEA can be flexibly implemented by countries prioritizing accounts based on availability of information and policy priorities. The accounts are designed to respond to data needs for multiple policy initiatives including global initiatives on sustainable development goals (SDGs), on mitigating and adapting to climate change, disaster related statistics and on measuring the contribution of the environment to well-being. The accounts are also a necessary input to the compilation of headline indicators such as net domestic product as part of the recently adopted 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA). / In Asia, good progress has been made in the compilation of SEEA accounts with many countries regularly compiling SEEA CF accounts. National statistical offices (NSOs) of countries in the region continue to express strong interest in compiling SEEA accounts, including taking steps towards compiling asset accounts which are relevant for informing the relationship between the economy and the environment. With the recent adoption of the 2025 SNA which has expanded its asset boundary to include several natural resources assets of the SEEA CF, demands for environmental asset accounts will increase as the SEEA CF can provide input data for the compilation of the 2025 SNA. More broadly, there is a need to strengthen the capacities of NSOs to produce and disseminate SEEA accounts to better meet the needs of users for high quality integrated data on the contribution of the environment to the economy and the impact of the economy on the environment.

title: titleUnited Nations Regional Workshop on the Implementation of the Degree of Urbanization Methodology, Kazakhstan, Almaty, 8-12 May 2023 /     DESA/Statistics Division conducted a capacity building training workshop on the Degree of Urbanisation (DEGURBA) Methodology for national statistics offices and geospatial institutions of countries in Central Asia.  /     The workshop was organized by DESA Statistics Division, in cooperation with the European Commission Joint Research Center (EC-JRC) and UN-Habitat. /     The participants were statisticians and geospatial specialists from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, as well as resource persons and experts from the Statistics Division, ESCAP, EC-JRC and UN-Habitat.  /     As national Statistical Offices use different national criteria to define cities, urban and rural areas, the Degree of Urbanisation methodology was developed by the European Commission, UN-Habitat, FAO and other partners as a way to harmonize these definitions and promote international and regional data comparability, particularly in the context of reporting on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and on the New Urban Agenda (NUA) indicators. DEGURBA was endorsed by the Statistical Commission at its 51st Session in 2020.  /     Through theoretical and practical sessions the participants were trained on 1) the need for this methodology 2) theory and concepts 3) data inputs, data preparation and technical capacity 4) applying the methodology, reviewing and evaluating the results and 5) its applications for reporting of data and SDG indicators by degree of urbanization. The participants also exchanged experiences and challenges and learned from each other. Finally, this capacity building workshop further emphasized and provided practical knowledge on the importance of integrating census data with geospatial information.  /     15 national participants as well as other expenses related to venue, catering and interpretation were funded by Statistics Division of DESA through financial contribution from a Eurostat Grant. Two staff members of Statistics Division of DESA were funded from RPTC funds. /     For more detailed information please find attached the report of the workshop.

The meeting helps develop the skills, knowledge, and technical foundations needed for advance in the implementation of environmentalâ€‘economic accounting in countries. Bringing together SEEA practitioners and compilers from several countries, along with experts from international organizations, the meeting serves as a platform for peer learning and exchange. Participants share best practices, discuss challenges, and learn directly from one anotherâ€™s experiences in compiling and using the SEEA. Through these collaborative learning opportunities, the meeting significantly contributes to building national and regional capacity in environmentalâ€‘economic accounting. / The concept note for the 2026 Joint meeting on Implementation of the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) is available here. / Back-to-back with the Joint Expert Meeting, UNSD will organize two-day meeting of the SEEA Central Framework Technical Committee on 23 and 27 March 2026, to advance the discussion of the issues for the update of the SEEA Central Framework.  / The organization of back-to-back meetings of the Technical Committee and the UNECE/OECD Expert Group will achieve significant synergies between the two meetings and allow Technical Committee members already attending the Joint UNECE/OECD Expert Meeting to also attend the Technical Committee meeting without incurring significant additional expenses, and vice versa.  / This activity will cover the participation of 6 participants from developing countries and 2 UNSD staff members to attend the Joint UNECE/OECD Expert Meeting and the Technical Committee meeting and. summary: In the series of regional capacity building workshops on Data Ethics, Governance, and Quality in a Changing Data Ecosystem since November 2024, many NSOs from developing countries pinpointed the increasing importance in upholding these principles to ensure official statistics remain credible, relevant, and responsive to complex and often compounded societal challenges. title: titleRequest 5280
summary: UNSD conducts an annual Global Assessment of Environmental-Economic Accounting and Supporting Statistics (https://seea.un.org/content/global-assessment-environmental-economic-accounting) to monitor the implementation of the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) in countries. This assessment provides critical insights into global progress and challenges in integrating environmental and economic data and is the basis for the monitoring of SDG indicator 15.9.1(b). While the number of countries implementing the SEEA has steadily increased since 2014, recent assessments indicate that this growth has plateaued, suggesting that many countries may be encountering persistent barriers to further implementation. / This stagnation underscores the urgent need to strengthen national capacities for compiling SEEA accounts. Many countries, particularly those in the early stages of implementation, face challenges related to technical expertise, institutional coordination, data availability, and methodological understanding. Addressing these challenges requires targeted support and knowledge exchange. The proposed activity will facilitate peer learning and collaboration among countries. Through the sharing of practical experiences, lessons learned, and innovative approaches, countries will gain valuable insights into overcoming common obstacles and advancing their SEEA implementation. / Target countries will learn from the sharing of country experiences in the compilation of environmental accounts of other countries and how those countries have addressed challenges both in the implementation of the accounts and in the developments of concepts, methods and tools to address these challenges. / This activity also facilitates South-South cooperation, enabling countries with similar development contexts to support one another. It promotes mutual learning, strengthens regional and global networks, and builds lasting partnerships. The London Group meetings, which attract a wide range of countries at various stages of SEEA implementation as well as key international organizations, provide an ideal platform for such an engagement. These meetings facilitate dialogue, encourage innovation, and help align national efforts with global standards and best practices. By building capacity through collaboration and shared learning, it empowers countries to produce high-quality environmental-economic accounts that inform sustainable development policies and contribute to achieving the SDGs.

title: titleThe mandate for the proposed activity comes from the resolution adopted by the 56th session of the United Nations Statistical Commission (to be adopted by Economic and Social Council later in 2025) on the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme as well as decision 56/102 of the Statistical Commission. Both the resolution and the decision recognize censuses as key for formulating, implementing, and monitoring inclusive socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability policies, and as a vital source of disaggregated data for tracking the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, including assessments by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location, and other characteristics. As part of the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme, which includes several inter-related objectives and activities, UNSD is mandated to develop international statistical standards, methods, and guidelines to facilitate the conduct of population and housing censuses, and to provide technical assistance for building national capacity in planning and conducting censuses.
summary: The request is for a capacity building workshop to prepare census managers in Anglophone African countries to successfully plan their 2030 round censuses and to effectively implement the Revision 4 of the United Nations Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (P&R Rev.4), endorsed by the 56th session of the Statistical Commission in March 2025. The primary objectives of the workshop include fostering a shared understanding of the updated global standards contained in the P&R Rev.4, enhancing participants' technical proficiencies in applying the revised recommendations (including areas like geospatial data, administrative records, new core topics, contingency planning, quality assurance, and communication), facilitating the exchange of best practices and collaborative problem-solving for anticipated challenges in the upcoming census round, and exploring innovative methodologies and opportunities for future administrative data-based censuses to improve efficiency and quality. / The workshop is jointly organized by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), the African Centre for Statistics at the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Statistics South Africa, and the Office of National Statistics of the United Kingdom (ONS-UK). Participants will include representatives from national statistical offices, such as census managers/coordinators or senior census staff responsible for census planning and implementation, as well as managers/senior technical experts in census operations, such as mapping, data processing, ICT or other relevant areas.

title: titleStatistical training is key to increasing the skills of staff at National Statistical Offices (NSOs) and the wider National Statistical System (NSS). In many low- and middle-income countries, there is, however, no systematic institutional plan in place to ensure the capacity development of staff. The Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) has developed the Statistical Training needs Assessment Tool (STAT) which the NSO can use to identify, prioritize, and meet training needs among staff and within the NSS. Before STAT was launched at the 55th UNSC, STAT was piloted in six countries with two countries (Ghana and Colombia) participating in a more thorough pilot. STAT is still a very new tool with a need to continue testing and thus learning from those countries who in this early phase decide to implement STAT. This includes among others learning more about the phase of developing an institutional training plan, how to implement it, and how to increase the use of e-learning and other non-classroom-based training.

summary: UNSD is preparing a use case to demonstrate the dissemination of data and the integration of SDG metadata into statistical outputs using the SDMX standard. This initiative focuses on linking SDG metadata with the UNdata mobile applications to enhance the accessibility and usability of statistical information. This use case can be used in workshops and guide participants through the process of extracting SDG data and metadata and integrating them into digital products. To support this, UNSD plans to update both UNdata Android and iOS apps with the latest available 2025 data - these updates will mirror the content of the printed Pocketbook publication. For each included SDG indicator, the apps will feature direct links to corresponding metadata, enabling users to explore definitions, methodologies, and sources seamlessly. / To ensure a fully functional and user-friendly experience, UNSD also plans to address several technical issues identified by both internal and external users in the SDG user interface, APIs and metadata related components of the system. This project not only enhances the visibility and utility of SDG data and metadata but also promotes best practices in data and metadata integration and digital dissemination using SDMX standards. / The proposal covers the contractual services needed to update the UNdata apps and fix some components in the SDG infrastructure, including SDG metadata.

title: titleUNSD in cooperation with other partners is regularly conducting trainings on the implementation of SDMX for data exchange and national data and metadata dissemination. In particular, many countries are lagging behind in the standard dissemination of their metadata. The integration of SDMX dissemination into digital products offers an opportunity to address this deficiency. In this proposal on the integration of SDG data and metadata into statistical outputs via SDMX, UNSD will implement a linkage of SDG data and metadata with the UNdata mobile app. / All global SDG data and metadata is available on UNSDâ€™s Global SDG Indicators Data Platform via SDMX APIs. In particular, the SDG metadata is disseminated through a SDMX API in a machine-readable format. A template is used to convert the metadata and the infrastructure behind is maintained by UNSD. The UNdata mobile app is a free app produced by the United Nations that gives users portable access to a compilation of key statistical indicators organized into 4 sections: general information, economic indicators, social indicators, environmental and infrastructure indicators for 30 geographical regions and over 200 countries and areas of the world. It responds to the General Assembly resolution 2626 (XXV), in which the Secretary-General has requested to supply basic national data that will increase international public awareness of countries' development efforts. The app is multilingual, and users can choose between English, French and Spanish.
summary: During this project, UNSD plans to update both apps, Android and iOS, with the 2024 data that are already available and whose content will fully resemble the printed version of the World Statistics Pocketbook 2024. For those SDG indicators included, a link to SDG data and metadata from the app will be added. In order to achieve this, UNSD plans to fix some shortcomings that external and internal users have identified in the SDG user interface including the API and other relevant parts of the system such as those related to the SDG metadata. These fixes will facilitate the integration and use of the SDG data and metadata links in the UNdata apps. / The budget will cover the contractual services needed to update the UNdata apps and fix some components in the SDG infrastructure, including SDG metadata. / UNSD will utilize this use case of the integration of SDG data and metadata into statistical outputs via SDMX in its forthcoming SDMX Regional Training Workshop organized and hosted by OECD in collaboration with other international agencies, including UNSD, SESRIC, ESCAP and UNESCO that will take place in Istanbul, TÃ¼rkiye, on 4-6 December 2024. Participants will be trained in the extraction of SDG data and metadata and its integration into digital products such as the UNdata apps.

title: titleThe General Assembly resolution 70/1 Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development calls for data that is â€œhigh-quality, accessible, timely, reliable and disaggregated by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migration status, disability and geographic location and other characteristics relevant in national contexts.â€ Improving interoperability, timeliness, and accessibility is key to the provision of data in support of evidence-based decision making. / Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange (SDMX) is an international standard that is extensively used for dissemination and reporting. In the European Union, national governments are legally obligated to report their statistical data to the European Commission in the SDMX format. Outside of the EU, countries are increasingly turning to SDMX to improve the quality and interoperability of their statistical dissemination and reporting while reducing the reporting burden.  / UNSD has long provided capacity building to the Member States in SDMX reporting and dissemination, particularly in the context of the MDGs and SDGs. As a result, many countries in Asia, Africa and the Middle East have established SDG dissemination platforms based on SDMX, and reported their data to UNSD, the Regional Commissions, and other parties. These activities have been primarily funded by extra-budgetary sources; more recently, RPTC has taken an increasingly important role, particularly in the context of a highly successful joint UNSD-ESCWA initiative that led to the establishment of SDMX-based reporting of SDG indicators in the Arab region. / The Workshop is being organized and hosted by OECD in collaboration with other international agencies, such as UNSD, SESRIC, ESCAP and UNESCO. It is planned to take place in Istanbul, TÃ¼rkiye, on 4-6 December 2024 (3 days).  / UNSD will bring to this workshop some Member States in response to the UN Statistical Commissionâ€™s request (E/2023/24-E/CN.3/2023/37) for more training in the subject matter. The workshop will move beyond basic concepts and will enable participants to strengthen their SDMX facilities for dissemination and reporting of data, including SDGs. The workshop will also facilitate interactive dialogue among the countries.
summary: The Workshop is being organized and hosted by OECD in collaboration with other international agencies, such as UNSD, SESRIC, ESCAP and UNESCO. title: titleStatistical training is key to increasing the skills of staff at National Statistical Offices (NSOs) and the wider National Statistical System (NSS). In many low- and middle-income countries, there is, however, no systematic institutional plan in place to ensure the capacity development of staff. The Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) has developed the Statistical Training needs Assessment Tool (STAT) which the NSO can use to identify, prioritize, and meet training needs among staff and within the NSS. Before STAT was launched at the 55th UNSC, STAT was piloted in six countries with two countries (Ghana and Colombia) participating in a more thorough pilot. STAT is still a very new tool with a need to continue testing and thus learning from those countries who in this early phase decide to implement STAT. This includes among others learning more about the phase of developing an institutional training plan, how to implement it, and how to increase the use of e-learning and other non-classroom-based training.

summary: Training Workshop on an Accounting Approach to Climate Change and Biodiversity in Central Asia and the Caucasus, 9-12 September 2024, Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan / Climate change and biodiversity loss are some of the most pressing policy issues globally, given their wide-ranging impacts on well-being. Many of the countries in the Central Asia and the Caucasus region are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change and biodiversity loss due to their geographic location. To effectively devise climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies and biodiversity loss prevention policies, countries in the region need reliable statistics and indicators on climate change impacts and biodiversity. These statistics and indicators also need to take into account the economic impacts of climate change and biodiversity, for example, the vulnerabilities of different economic sectors to climate impacts and or the state of ecosystems and the ecosystem services they provide. Integrated statistics on the environment-economy nexus will ensure that countries in the region can create policies which mitigate and adapt to climate change and biodiversity loss while strengthening their economies. / National statistical offices in the region are well placed to produce statistics on the environment-economy nexus, which can be compiled according to the international statistical standard, the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA). At the same time, there is a need to strengthen their capabilities to produce and disseminate related statistics and indicators to better meet user needs. This workshop will cover SEEA energy and air emission accounts, and ecosystem accounts to support the compilation of indicators relevant to climate change and biodiversity. It will also cover dissemination practices and institutional mechanisms needed to strengthen the institutions producing these statistics. / The target audience are officials from national statistical offices, ministries of environment and experts from other relevant government agencies, from the nine countries that will be invited to the will be invited to the Workshop, namely Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

summary: The request is based on an overall demand from National Statistical Systems (NSS) overall in developing countries for support in producing more timely and disaggregated SDG indicators as well as information on COVID-19 using administrative data for statistical purposes. As a response to this, the Collaborative on Administrative Data was established in June 2020. It was presented to the UN Statistical Commission in March 2021, also based on earlier requests from the Commission in earlier years and through the Inter-Agency Expert Group on SDGs (IAEG-SDG). It received strong endorsement and support from the UN Statistical Commission in 2021. / Overall, there is a strong need to increase the knowledge on how to better make use of administrative data for statistics production in countries.. If such data sources are of sufficient quality, they reduce response burden on the population, reduce data collection costs and they may give a more complete and disaggregated picture of a situation than other sources. Many countries are, however, still struggling to use this source of data and through the Collaborative (and before that through a number of other channels), they have expressed a strong need for capacity development and training support. As part of the Collaborative, there has been much work, led by the countries that are members of the Collaborative, to collect currently available guidance, and where lacking, specifying needs for additional practical tools and guidance materials. As members, including international partners, have limited capacity to respond to these requests for practical guidance tools, it is, among others, proposed to hire consultant(s) who can support the work and help it progress more quickly. That way, countries will also be able to increase their efforts to provide more timely and disaggregated information on the SDGs and COVID-19 / This has mainly taken place through informal online meetings orally with no formal meeting minutes and cant therefore be attached as files to this request.   / An overview of the Collaborative and the task teams can be found here: https://unstats.un.org/capacity-development/admin-data/

summary: The Financing for Sustainable Development Office (FSDO) of the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) organized a Regional Workshop on Transfer Pricing in Asia-Pacific, held from 25 to 29 August 2025 in Incheon, Republic of Korea.  / The workshop responded directly to countries' demand for practical tools and training on transfer pricing, aimed at strengthening domestic resource mobilization to support sustainable development. Transfer pricing â€” the pricing of cross-border transactions involving goods, services, or intangibles between related entitiesâ€” has gained increasing global attention due to its significant implications for equitable taxation and sustainable development.  / Developing countries face considerable challenges in this area, including a high risk of profit shifting and limited access to specialized training and resources available to policy makers and tax administrations. title: titleThe mandate for the proposed activity comes from the resolution adopted by the 56th session of the United Nations Statistical Commission (to be adopted by Economic and Social Council later in 2025) on the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme as well as decision 56/102 of the Statistical Commission. Both the resolution and the decision recognize censuses as key for formulating, implementing, and monitoring inclusive socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability policies, and as a vital source of disaggregated data for tracking the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, including assessments by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location, and other characteristics. As part of the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme, which includes several inter-related objectives and activities, UNSD is mandated to develop international statistical standards, methods, and guidelines to facilitate the conduct of population and housing censuses, and to provide technical assistance for building national capacity in planning and conducting censuses.
summary: The request is for a capacity building workshop to prepare census managers in Asian countries to successfully plan their 2030 round censuses and to effectively implement the Revision 4 of the United Nations Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (P&R Rev.4), endorsed by the 56th session of the Statistical Commission in March 2025. The primary objectives of the workshop include fostering a shared understanding of the updated global standards contained in the P&R Rev.4, enhancing participants' technical proficiencies in applying the revised recommendations (including areas like geospatial data, administrative records, new core topics, contingency planning, quality assurance, and communication), facilitating the exchange of best practices and collaborative problem-solving for anticipated challenges in the upcoming census round, and exploring innovative methodologies and opportunities for future administrative data-based censuses to improve efficiency and quality. / The workshop is jointly organized by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), the United Nations Statistical Institute for Asia and the Pacific (SIAP), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), and the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). Participants will include representatives from national statistical offices, such as census managers/coordinators or senior census staff responsible for census planning and implementation, as well as managers/senior technical experts in census operations, such as mapping, data processing, ICT or other relevant areas.

title: titleUNSD in cooperation with other partners is regularly conducting trainings on the implementation of SDMX for data exchange and national data and metadata dissemination. In particular, many countries are lagging behind in the standard dissemination of their metadata. The integration of SDMX dissemination into digital products offers an opportunity to address this deficiency. In this proposal on the integration of SDG data and metadata into statistical outputs via SDMX, UNSD will implement a linkage of SDG data and metadata with the UNdata mobile app. / All global SDG data and metadata is available on UNSDâ€™s Global SDG Indicators Data Platform via SDMX APIs. In particular, the SDG metadata is disseminated through a SDMX API in a machine-readable format. A template is used to convert the metadata and the infrastructure behind is maintained by UNSD. The UNdata mobile app is a free app produced by the United Nations that gives users portable access to a compilation of key statistical indicators organized into 4 sections: general information, economic indicators, social indicators, environmental and infrastructure indicators for 30 geographical regions and over 200 countries and areas of the world. It responds to the General Assembly resolution 2626 (XXV), in which the Secretary-General has requested to supply basic national data that will increase international public awareness of countries' development efforts. The app is multilingual, and users can choose between English, French and Spanish.
summary: During this project, UNSD plans to update both apps, Android and iOS, with the 2024 data that are already available and whose content will fully resemble the printed version of the World Statistics Pocketbook 2024. In the European Union, national governments are legally obligated to report their statistical data to the European Commission in the SDMX format. Outside of the EU, countries are increasingly turning to SDMX to improve the quality and interoperability of their statistical dissemination and reporting while reducing the reporting burden.  / UNSD has long provided capacity building to the Member States in SDMX reporting and dissemination, particularly in the context of the MDGs and SDGs. These activities have been primarily funded by extra-budgetary sources; more recently, RPTC has taken an increasingly important role, particularly in the context of a highly successful joint UNSD-ESCWA initiative that led to the establishment of SDMX-based reporting of SDG indicators in the Arab region. / The Workshop is being organized and hosted by OECD in collaboration with other international agencies, such as UNSD, SESRIC, ESCAP and UNESCO.
