title: titleFSDO will carry out research into the digitalization of tax administration processes in response to a request by the Iranian National Tax Administration (INTA) (letter from INTA to FSDO is attached in this demand repository). Iran is interested to see how other countries have gone about the process of digitalizing revenue administration processes with a view to learning from the experiences and best practices towards establishing a â€˜smart tax systemâ€™.  / Digitalization of processes can be one of the most effective mechanisms to enhance revenue collection and enforcement, as it will improve efficiency and effectiveness of tax collection. These processes can play an important role in reducing risk and building resilience by strengthening developing countries tax enforcement and collection mechanisms to enhance revenue generation and administration, thereby supporting these countriesâ€™ domestic resource mobilization efforts for the achievement of the SDGs.  / FSDO has considered the request by INTA and finds that the research will be useful not only for Iran but for other developing countries in the midst of or considering digitalizing their tax administration processes. Moreover, the work will be beneficial for the UN Tax Committeeâ€™s small group on digitalization of tax processes, which is anticipated to inform future UN capacity development work in this area.  / Accordingly, the research would cover the following aspects from the digitalization of tax administrations perspective: (i) the definition of/criteria for determining a smart tax system; (ii) the role and position of different departments/units (such as information technology) within the tax administration in the process of digitalization; (iii) the role of other government departments in the digitalization process; and (iv) examples of countries that have successfully implemented smart tax systems.  / In the Outcome document of the 2022 Financing for Development (FfD) Forum, Member States recommitted to strengthening the capacities of revenue administration through modernized, transparent and progressive tax systems, improved tax policy and more efficient tax collection (E/FFDF/2022/L.1, p. 4.). To this end, Member States called upon the international community to scale up support for capacity-building to developing countries, especially in building their tax policy and administration capacities. In resolution 68/204 of 20 December 2013 (A/RES/68/204), the General Assembly recalled the commitment of Member States to enhance and strengthen domestic resource mobilization and fiscal space, including through modernized tax systems and the broadening of tax base. The same resolution reiterated the importance of supporting national efforts in these areas by strengthening technical assistance and enhancing international cooperation and participation in addressing international tax matters.  / In response to the request of the INTA, UNDESA commissioned a general research paper on relevant, specified aspects of the digitalization of tax administration processes. In June 2023, DESA shared the research paper with the Tax Administration, which introduces the subject and lays out key considerations for tax authorities in the journey to digitalizing their tax administrations. For reference, a short note from UNDESA was also sent to the INTA summarizing some aspects of the structure of the paper.
summary: The request was initiated by Iran, but it will help other developing countries understand specific aspects of the digitalization of tax administration processes to mitigate risk, build resilience and enforce revenue collection to finance the SDGs.

title: titleReport of 55th Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2024), decision 55/109 (h): / o	The Statistical Commission supported the efforts of international organizations, regional commissions and statistical training institutes in providing technical assistance, organizing workshops and training and developing compilation tools, and noted the importance of ensuring that resources continue to be made available for this work  / Report of the 50th Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2019), decision 50/115 (c): / o	The Statistical Commission requested the Committee of Experts to continue its work on mainstreaming the use of SEEA for policy processes, in particular with regards to biodiversity, in view of the adoption of the post-2020 biodiversity agenda, and climate change, circular economy, beyond gross domestic product (GDP) and green growth initiatives / Report of the 42nd Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2011), para. 105 (a), (b), (c): / o	The Statistical Commission welcomed with appreciation the report of the Secretary General on energy statistics (E/CN.3/2011/8) and noted that the work undertaken on the international recommendations for energy statistics illustrates effective cooperation among different agencies, expert groups and countries; adopted the international recommendations for energy statistics; endorsed the main elements of the proposed implementation programme
summary: Climate change is one of the most pressing policy issues around the world, with all countries being vulnerable to its adverse effects. To better mitigate climate change, countries are more and more looking to understand how to use energy more effectively and sustainably. Such an understanding requires countries to have high-quality energy statistics, balances and accounts. Together, energy statistics, balances and accounts can provide governments with the data they need to understand how the energy sector can be made more efficient and sustainable; how the economy can be made more energy efficient; and how changes in energy use can contribute to fewer emissions. ESCWA countries have expressed interest in capacity building on energy statistics and accounts. In addition, according to the 2023 Global Assessment on Environmental-Economic Accounting, Jordan plans to restart compilation of System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) accounts; Morocco and Tunisia have plans to expand its compilation of SEEA accounts; and Somalia has plans to begin compilation of SEEA accounts. / National statistical offices are well placed to produce energy statistics, balances and accounts. Energy statistics and balances can be compiled according to the International Recommendations for Energy Statistics (IRES), and energy accounts can be compiled according to the international statistical standard, the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA). At the same time, there is a need to strengthen the capacity of national statistical offices and other relevant ministries to produce and disseminate energy statistics, balances and accounts to better meet user needs.  / UNSD, in collaboration with ESCWA, SESRIC, IEA and AITRS held the workshop, "Energy Statistics, Balances and Accounts for Informed Energy and Climate Policies" from 10-12 December in Ankara. More than 40 participants from national statistical offices and ministries of energy came together from 10-12 December 2024 in Ankara to build capacity compilation and use of energy statistics, balances and accounts to support the dissemination of high-quality data for energy and climate change policies. The workshop also covered the institutional mechanisms needed to strengthen the institutions producing these statistics and allowed countries to share their experiences.

title: titleEndorsed by the United Nations Statistical Commission in June 2008, SDMX is recognized as a preferred standard for data and its related meta-information, has been approved as an ISO standard (17369:2013). In its most recent report E/2023/24-E/CN.3/2023/37, as well as previous reports, the United Nations Statistical Commission expressed its appreciation for the progressed made by the Working Group and encouraged more capacity development efforts in this area. / This workshop is organized jointly with ESCWA for the Arab region countries. ESCWA will co-facilitate and co-fund the event including additional countries. / The workshop took place 5-8 June 2023 in Amman, Jordan.

The participants will share national experiences on implementing automated data and metadata exchange for statistical indicators using the ESCWA SDMX Converter. The Workshop will be organized for a duration of four days (5th June- 8th June 2023) and will include presentations, demonstrations, and Q&A sessions, and hands-on exercises as a main focus of this course.

title: titleRequest 5280
summary: UNSD conducts an annual Global Assessment of Environmental-Economic Accounting and Supporting Statistics (https://seea.un.org/content/global-assessment-environmental-economic-accounting) to monitor the implementation of the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) in countries. This assessment provides critical insights into global progress and challenges in integrating environmental and economic data and is the basis for the monitoring of SDG indicator 15.9.1(b). While the number of countries implementing the SEEA has steadily increased since 2014, recent assessments indicate that this growth has plateaued, suggesting that many countries may be encountering persistent barriers to further implementation. / This stagnation underscores the urgent need to strengthen national capacities for compiling SEEA accounts. Many countries, particularly those in the early stages of implementation, face challenges related to technical expertise, institutional coordination, data availability, and methodological understanding. Addressing these challenges requires targeted support and knowledge exchange. The proposed activity will facilitate peer learning and collaboration among countries. Through the sharing of practical experiences, lessons learned, and innovative approaches, countries will gain valuable insights into overcoming common obstacles and advancing their SEEA implementation. / Target countries will learn from the sharing of country experiences in the compilation of environmental accounts of other countries and how those countries have addressed challenges both in the implementation of the accounts and in the developments of concepts, methods and tools to address these challenges. / This activity also facilitates South-South cooperation, enabling countries with similar development contexts to support one another. It promotes mutual learning, strengthens regional and global networks, and builds lasting partnerships. The London Group meetings, which attract a wide range of countries at various stages of SEEA implementation as well as key international organizations, provide an ideal platform for such an engagement. These meetings facilitate dialogue, encourage innovation, and help align national efforts with global standards and best practices. By building capacity through collaboration and shared learning, it empowers countries to produce high-quality environmental-economic accounts that inform sustainable development policies and contribute to achieving the SDGs.

title: titleUnited Nations Regional Workshop on the Implementation of the Degree of Urbanization Methodology, Kazakhstan, Almaty, 8-12 May 2023 /     DESA/Statistics Division conducted a capacity building training workshop on the Degree of Urbanisation (DEGURBA) Methodology for national statistics offices and geospatial institutions of countries in Central Asia.  /     The workshop was organized by DESA Statistics Division, in cooperation with the European Commission Joint Research Center (EC-JRC) and UN-Habitat. /     The participants were statisticians and geospatial specialists from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, as well as resource persons and experts from the Statistics Division, ESCAP, EC-JRC and UN-Habitat.  /     As national Statistical Offices use different national criteria to define cities, urban and rural areas, the Degree of Urbanisation methodology was developed by the European Commission, UN-Habitat, FAO and other partners as a way to harmonize these definitions and promote international and regional data comparability, particularly in the context of reporting on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and on the New Urban Agenda (NUA) indicators. DEGURBA was endorsed by the Statistical Commission at its 51st Session in 2020.  /     Through theoretical and practical sessions the participants were trained on 1) the need for this methodology 2) theory and concepts 3) data inputs, data preparation and technical capacity 4) applying the methodology, reviewing and evaluating the results and 5) its applications for reporting of data and SDG indicators by degree of urbanization. The participants also exchanged experiences and challenges and learned from each other. Finally, this capacity building workshop further emphasized and provided practical knowledge on the importance of integrating census data with geospatial information.  /     15 national participants as well as other expenses related to venue, catering and interpretation were funded by Statistics Division of DESA through financial contribution from a Eurostat Grant. Two staff members of Statistics Division of DESA were funded from RPTC funds. /     For more detailed information please find attached the report of the workshop.
summary: Statistics Divisionâ€™s Demographic and Social Statistics Branch will conduct a regional workshop with UN-Habitat and European Commission on the implementation of the Degree of Urbanisation (DEGURBA) methodology. This methodology is endorsed by the Statistical Commission at its 51st Session as a definition of cities, urban and rural areas for statistical comparison purposes.  An implementation manual of the DEGURBA methodology was presented as a background document to the Statistical Commission at its 52nd Session. Implementation of this methodology will serve reporting of several SDG indicators having an urban/city and rural dimension in a harmonized manner among countries. The workshop is planned to take place in Kazakhstan, Almaty, during 8-12 May 2023.

summary: Time-use statistics provide a critical lens for understanding how people allocate their time across paid work, unpaid care, and other activities, offering insights into well-being that go beyond traditional economic indicators. These data are essential for monitoring SDG indicator 5.4.1 on unpaid care and domestic work and are increasingly relevant in Beyond GDP discussions. / Existing international standards and tools, developed under the UNSD time-use statistics programme and endorsed by the Statistical Commission, provide a strong foundation for this work. These include the International Classification of Activities for Time-Use Statistics (ICATUS), the Guide to Producing Statistics on Time Use, and the Minimum Harmonized Instrument (MHI), which together ensure comparable, high-quality data across countries. The consultancy will develop user-friendly training materials to support national statistical offices in applying these standards, operationalizing the MHI, and producing reliable and comparable time-use statistics. / The training materials will enhance capacities in understanding international standards, operationalizing the MHI, and linking ICATUS and MHI activity lists for calculating SDG Indicator 5.4.1. They will be designed for hybrid, in-person, and online workshops, as well as userâ€“producer dialogues. This activity supports gender equality, human rights, disability inclusion, and the Leave No One Behind principle by generating disaggregated data that inform inclusive and evidence-based policies. / A total RPTC budget of US$20,000 is proposed to cover the consultancy fee for the development of these training materials, which will serve as a practical resource for statisticians

summary: Through the work of the Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) it has been re-confirmed that there is a continued urgent need to support developing countries in creating and better maintaining statistical training programs at national level. This is key for staff at the National Statistical Systems (NSS) to receive core trainings for doing their jobs efficiently, and will make the NSS less dependent on external partners. / GIST has identified that a key step is to help countries develop a needs assessment tool to understand the training needs of their staff as well as key development area needs from a managerial perspective. In relation to this, there is also a need to provide guidance on how to prioritize among gaps identified. / GIST members are actively supporting the work, but are in needs of support in coordinating the work, helping it move forward more quickly to respond to countries needs and ultimately help staff in the NSS improve their skills more systematically to increase efficiency of the NSS in providing quality and timely SDG and other statistics to the public. / GIST has developed the Statistical Training needs Assessment Tool (STAT) which NSOs can use to identify, prioritize, and meet training needs among staff and within the NSS. STAT is still a relatively new tool with a need to continued testing and improving and thus learning from countries who decide to implement STAT. The STAT tool code needs now an update to make it language-agnostic and allow for easier translation of the tool and surveys into any language. This will significantly increase the accessibility and usability of STAT for countries worldwide, particularly in non-English speaking regions. / The enhanced STAT tool then needs to be piloted in countries that have expressed their interest in implementing STAT. At this moment Argentina, Djibouti, State of Palestine, and Viet Nam have already expressed that interest, with possibly additional countries joining. / The results from the pilots, along with additional inputs from GIST members, should then be reflected in a revision of the chapter on Human Resources Management and Training of the Handbook on Management and Organisation of National Statistical Systems. / See also previous reference number: 4234

See below email content: / "EAPD run a global macro-econometric model (known as the World Economic and Forecasting Model (or WEFM) to generate short-term (t+1 and t+2) growth forecasts for more than 170 countries and territories world-wide. Individual country forecasts of the model are linked via a trade matrix that equilibrates global export and import volumes and prices. EAPD is  able to fine-tune and calibrate individual country models depending on the availability of data and other country-specific or other idiosyncratic factors. WEFM is not a  policy model. As such, it does not contain policy variables â€“ such as interest rate, tariff or tax rates â€“ that can be tweaked to assess the impact of a particular policy choice. EAPD is, however, able to introduce shocks to the structural variables (many of them can be proxies for underlying policy variables) and trace their pass-through effects. Lately, EAPD added a poverty module to run medium-term poverty headcount forecasts that triangulates growth, income distribution and poverty. The choice of a particular model, and its feasibility, depends on what the policymakers in Tajikistan have in mind and their expectations from a model. If they are looking for a growth forecasting model, EAPD would be happy to share the WEFM files for Tajikistan. The government partners or the RCO would, however, need the EViews statistical package and requisite skills to run the model. If they are looking for a policy model to simulate policy outcomes, WEFM is perhaps not the optimal choice. Modelling framework such as the GTAP (or other CGE models) may be considered. RCO may also consider looking at optimization models â€“ such as the CLEWS â€“ which allows policymakers to choose an optimal path (e.g. regarding the use of water or energy resources) to achieve a given objective. Should there be any interest in an optimization model (e.g. CLEWS), EAPD  may be in a position to provide necessary capacity development support". / No feedback from Government or RCO. The assumption is that they chose a different model

title: titleRequest 3989
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic presented a major challenge for household survey programmes. Traditional face-to-face survey operations have become difficult to implement in many countries due to social distancing requirements and other restriction measures as a result of the pandemic. According to a survey conducted by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD) and the World Bank in May 2020, 96â€¯percent of national statistical offices (NSOs) partially or fully stopped face-to-face data collection. / In response to the government requirement on social distancing, many national statistical offices (NSOs) quickly turned to telephone or web interviews as an alternative data collection mode to maintain continuity in the production of key indicators and monitor the health and socio-economic impact of the pandemic.    / In the fourth round of UNSD and the World Bank survey of national statistical offices in May-June 2021, a marked increase was observed in the number of countries declaring a full resumption of face-to-face data collection activities. Globally 44 percent of the surveyed countries resumed full face-to-face data collection, compared to just four percent a year earlier. / While the adaptation of national household survey operations indicated the resilience of NSOs, such adaptation also raised challenges for countries on survey data quality. Change of survey data collection mode from face-to-face to telephone or web may impact on sample coverage, response rate and measurement error. Shortening survey questionnaires and changing question flows will also impact on the quality and comparability of survey data.   / In close consultation with the Task Force on COVID-19, established by the Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Household Surveys (ISWGHS), UNSD is hiring a consultant to develop a Guidance Note on Assessing and Minimizing the COVID Impact on Survey Quality.

title: titleRequest 3974
summary: In committing to the realization of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, Member States recognized that the dignity of the individuals is fundamental and that the Agendaâ€™s Goals and targets should be met for all nations and people and for all segments of society. Ensuring that these commitments are translated into effective action requires a precise understanding of the target populations and progress made in addressing their particular priorities.  / To properly measure this, statistics need to be presented for different population groups and geographical areas. The Global Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator framework has included an overarching principle of data disaggregation: Sustainable Development Goal indicators should be disaggregated, where relevant, by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability and geographic location, or other characteristics, in accordance with the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics.  / Small area estimation (SAE) techniques have been proved to be very useful to provide reliable disaggregated data for some SDG indicators, such as poverty estimation, food insecurity and undernutrition, health related indicators, unemployment rate, etc.   / Under the guidance of IAEG-SDGs and ISWGHS, a draft set of Toolkit has been developed by UNSD on small area estimation for SDGs.  The Toolkit provides guidance to countries, based on national experiences, on the use of small area estimation for SDG data disaggregation.  The Toolkit covers essential elements of the use of small area estimation including the use of input data, modelling, data validation and dissemination. The Toolkit also provides practical guidance to countries on how to move from SAE experiments to official production.   / In this regard, the UN Statistics Division (as the secretariat of both the Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Household Surveys and IAEG-SDGs working on SAE) is (a) fianlising the SAE Toolkit for SDG data disaggregation; and (b) developing a set of eLearning courses on small area estimation for SDGs data disaggregation, in collaboration with ECLAC Statistics Division and UNFPA .

summary: Through the work of the Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) it has been re-confirmed that there is an urgent need to support developing countries in creating and better maintaining statistical training programs at national level. This is key for staff at the National Statistical Systems (NSS) to receive core trainings for doing their jobs efficiently, and will make the NSS less dependent on external partners. / GIST has identified that a key first step is to help countries develop a needs assessment tool to understand the training needs of their staff as well as key development area needs from a managerial perspective. In relation to this, there is also a need to provide guidance on how to prioritise among gaps identified as well as to provide template curriculums for courses that are expected to be core in all countries. / GIST members are actively supporting the work, but are in needs of support in coordinating the work, helping it move forward more quickly to respond to countries needs and ultimately help staff in the NSS improve their skills more systematically to increase efficiency of the NSS in providing quality and timely SDG and other statistics to the public.

title: titleStatistical training is key to increasing the skills of staff at National Statistical Offices (NSOs) and the wider National Statistical System (NSS). In many low- and middle-income countries, there is, however, no systematic institutional plan in place to ensure the capacity development of staff. The Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) has developed the Statistical Training needs Assessment Tool (STAT) which the NSO can use to identify, prioritize, and meet training needs among staff and within the NSS. Before STAT was launched at the 55th UNSC, STAT was piloted in six countries with two countries (Ghana and Colombia) participating in a more thorough pilot. STAT is still a very new tool with a need to continue testing and thus learning from those countries who in this early phase decide to implement STAT. This includes among others learning more about the phase of developing an institutional training plan, how to implement it, and how to increase the use of e-learning and other non-classroom-based training.
summary: Following the presentation of STAT (see notes above) at the UN Statistical Commission in 2024, a number of countries have contacted UNSD and other GIST members as they want to implement STAT in their countries (all those listed in this demand proposal). summary: The technical workshop on time, places, people and relationships to organize social and demographic outcomes and statistics is organized by UNSD and hosted by Statistics Canada.  / The workshop aims to: / â€¢	Enhance national capacities, particularly in developing countries, to test and operationalize the building blocks TIME, PLACES, PEOPLE and RELATIONSHIPS as a lens to better organize social and demographic outcomes and statistics. / â€¢	Promote a shared understanding of the conceptual framework being advanced by the Friends of the Chair Group on Social and Demographic Statistics and how it can be applied to organize social and demographic statistics  in a coherent and integrated manner; / â€¢	Refine the conceptual framework based on national experiences, technical inputs, and emerging user needs; / â€¢	Exchange national experiences and innovations in data production, integration, and dissemination that align with the proposed framework, including practical applications, institutional arrangements, and lessons learned; / â€¢	Identify technical and operational priorities for piloting and implementing the new approach at the national level, including tools, guidance, capacity-building needs, and opportunities for collaboration; / â€¢	Strengthen the alignment of the conceptual framework with global agendas, including the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Pact for the Future, and initiatives to develop new measures of progress beyond GDP; / â€¢	Foster partnerships and peer learning among national statistical offices, regional and international organizations, and other stakeholders to support coherent implementation and promote long-term sustainability of the approach. / The Statistical Commission in its decision 55/112 (E/2024/24-E/CN.3/2024/36 ), endorsed the revised Guide to Producing Statistics on Time Use; took note of the interest expressed by countries in using the proposed methods, and requested the Statistics Division and partners to support countries in the implementation of the Guide, in collaboration with regional actors, to ensure its national relevance and effective implementation. title: titleBased on the intergovernmental agreed guidance by the UN Forum on Forests (UNFF), the UNFF-Global Forest Financing Facilitation Network (GFFFN) should maintain a list of country requests, provide support whenever capacity and resources become available. summary: The request is based on an overall demand from National Statistical Systems (NSS) overall in developing countries for support in producing more timely and disaggregated SDG indicators as well as information on COVID-19 using administrative data for statistical purposes. As a response to this, the Collaborative on Administrative Data was established in June 2020. It was presented to the UN Statistical Commission in March 2021, also based on earlier requests from the Commission in earlier years and through the Inter-Agency Expert Group on SDGs (IAEG-SDG). It received strong endorsement and support from the UN Statistical Commission in 2021. / Overall, there is a strong need to increase the knowledge on how to better make use of administrative data for statistics production in countries.. If such data sources are of sufficient quality, they reduce response burden on the population, reduce data collection costs and they may give a more complete and disaggregated picture of a situation than other sources. Many countries are, however, still struggling to use this source of data and through the Collaborative (and before that through a number of other channels), they have expressed a strong need for capacity development and training support. As part of the Collaborative, there has been much work, led by the countries that are members of the Collaborative, to collect currently available guidance, and where lacking, specifying needs for additional practical tools and guidance materials. As members, including international partners, have limited capacity to respond to these requests for practical guidance tools, it is, among others, proposed to hire consultant(s) who can support the work and help it progress more quickly. That way, countries will also be able to increase their efforts to provide more timely and disaggregated information on the SDGs and COVID-19 / This has mainly taken place through informal online meetings orally with no formal meeting minutes and cant therefore be attached as files to this request.   / An overview of the Collaborative and the task teams can be found here: https://unstats.un.org/capacity-development/admin-data/

title: titleThe mandate for the proposed activity comes from the resolution adopted by the 56th session of the United Nations Statistical Commission (to be adopted by Economic and Social Council later in 2025) on the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme as well as decision 56/102 of the Statistical Commission. Both the resolution and the decision recognize censuses as key for formulating, implementing, and monitoring inclusive socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability policies, and as a vital source of disaggregated data for tracking the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, including assessments by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location, and other characteristics. As part of the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme, which includes several inter-related objectives and activities, UNSD is mandated to develop international statistical standards, methods, and guidelines to facilitate the conduct of population and housing censuses, and to provide technical assistance for building national capacity in planning and conducting censuses.
summary: The request is for a capacity building workshop to prepare census managers in Pacific countries to successfully plan their 2030 round censuses and to effectively implement the Revision 4 of the United Nations Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (P&R Rev.4), endorsed by the 56th session of the Statistical Commission in March 2025. The primary objectives of the workshop include fostering a shared understanding of the updated global standards contained in the P&R Rev.4, enhancing participants' technical proficiencies in applying the revised recommendations (including areas like geospatial data, administrative records, new core topics, contingency planning, quality assurance, and communication), facilitating the exchange of best practices and collaborative problem-solving for anticipated challenges in the upcoming census round, and exploring innovative methodologies and opportunities for future administrative data-based censuses to improve efficiency and quality. / The workshop is jointly organized by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), the Pacific Community (SPC), the United Nations Statistical Institute for Asia and the Pacific (SIAP), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), and the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). Participants will include representatives from national statistical offices, such as census managers/coordinators or senior census staff responsible for census planning and implementation, as well as managers/senior technical experts in census operations, such as mapping, data processing, ICT or other relevant areas.

title: titleFSDO will organize two 2-day regional workshops on strengthening the capacity of developing countries to design risk-informed and data driven development cooperation strategies and policies in support of their COVID-19 response and recovery efforts. Each workshop will focus on a specific â€œenablerâ€ of effective development cooperation that has been identified by countries within the region as priorities for strengthening â€“ specifically, national development cooperation policies (NDCPs) in Africa and development cooperation information systems (DCIS) in Asia-Pacific.  / The biennial DCF Survey exercise and High-level Meeting of ECOSOCâ€™s Development Cooperation Forum serve as core activities through which developing countriesâ€™ capacity gaps and demand for learning and knowledge exchange are communicated. title: titleRequest 3974
summary: In committing to the realization of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, Member States recognized that the dignity of the individuals is fundamental and that the Agendaâ€™s Goals and targets should be met for all nations and people and for all segments of society. Ensuring that these commitments are translated into effective action requires a precise understanding of the target populations and progress made in addressing their particular priorities.  / To properly measure this, statistics need to be presented for different population groups and geographical areas. The Global Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator framework has included an overarching principle of data disaggregation: Sustainable Development Goal indicators should be disaggregated, where relevant, by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability and geographic location, or other characteristics, in accordance with the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics.  / Small area estimation (SAE) techniques have been proved to be very useful to provide reliable disaggregated data for some SDG indicators, such as poverty estimation, food insecurity and undernutrition, health related indicators, unemployment rate, etc.   / Under the guidance of IAEG-SDGs and ISWGHS, a draft set of Toolkit has been developed by UNSD on small area estimation for SDGs.  The Toolkit provides guidance to countries, based on national experiences, on the use of small area estimation for SDG data disaggregation.  The Toolkit covers essential elements of the use of small area estimation including the use of input data, modelling, data validation and dissemination. The Toolkit also provides practical guidance to countries on how to move from SAE experiments to official production.   / In this regard, the UN Statistics Division (as the secretariat of both the Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Household Surveys and IAEG-SDGs working on SAE) is (a) fianlising the SAE Toolkit for SDG data disaggregation; and (b) developing a set of eLearning courses on small area estimation for SDGs data disaggregation, in collaboration with ECLAC Statistics Division and UNFPA .

summary: The request is based on an overall demand from National Statistical Systems (NSS) overall in developing countries for support in producing more timely and disaggregated SDG indicators as well as information on COVID-19 using administrative data for statistical purposes. As a response to this, the Collaborative on Administrative Data was established in June 2020. It was presented to the UN Statistical Commission in March 2021, also based on earlier requests from the Commission in earlier years and through the Inter-Agency Expert Group on SDGs (IAEG-SDG). It received strong endorsement and support from the UN Statistical Commission in 2021. / Overall, there is a strong need to increase the knowledge on how to better make use of administrative data for statistics production in countries.. If such data sources are of sufficient quality, they reduce response burden on the population, reduce data collection costs and they may give a more complete and disaggregated picture of a situation than other sources. Many countries are, however, still struggling to use this source of data and through the Collaborative (and before that through a number of other channels), they have expressed a strong need for capacity development and training support. As part of the Collaborative, there has been much work, led by the countries that are members of the Collaborative, to collect currently available guidance, and where lacking, specifying needs for additional practical tools and guidance materials. As members, including international partners, have limited capacity to respond to these requests for practical guidance tools, it is, among others, proposed to hire consultant(s) who can support the work and help it progress more quickly. That way, countries will also be able to increase their efforts to provide more timely and disaggregated information on the SDGs and COVID-19 / This has mainly taken place through informal online meetings orally with no formal meeting minutes and cant therefore be attached as files to this request.   / An overview of the Collaborative and the task teams can be found here: https://unstats.un.org/capacity-development/admin-data/

title: titleThe mandate for the proposed activity comes from the resolution adopted by the 56th session of the United Nations Statistical Commission (to be adopted by Economic and Social Council later in 2025) on the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme as well as decision 56/102 of the Statistical Commission. Both the resolution and the decision recognize censuses as key for formulating, implementing, and monitoring inclusive socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability policies, and as a vital source of disaggregated data for tracking the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, including assessments by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location, and other characteristics. As part of the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme, which includes several inter-related objectives and activities, UNSD is mandated to develop international statistical standards, methods, and guidelines to facilitate the conduct of population and housing censuses, and to provide technical assistance for building national capacity in planning and conducting censuses.
summary: The request is for a capacity building workshop to prepare census managers in Pacific countries to successfully plan their 2030 round censuses and to effectively implement the Revision 4 of the United Nations Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (P&R Rev.4), endorsed by the 56th session of the Statistical Commission in March 2025. The primary objectives of the workshop include fostering a shared understanding of the updated global standards contained in the P&R Rev.4, enhancing participants' technical proficiencies in applying the revised recommendations (including areas like geospatial data, administrative records, new core topics, contingency planning, quality assurance, and communication), facilitating the exchange of best practices and collaborative problem-solving for anticipated challenges in the upcoming census round, and exploring innovative methodologies and opportunities for future administrative data-based censuses to improve efficiency and quality. / The workshop is jointly organized by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), the Pacific Community (SPC), the United Nations Statistical Institute for Asia and the Pacific (SIAP), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), and the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). Participants will include representatives from national statistical offices, such as census managers/coordinators or senior census staff responsible for census planning and implementation, as well as managers/senior technical experts in census operations, such as mapping, data processing, ICT or other relevant areas.

summary: The Statistical Commission requested the development partners to continue to support capacity development to strengthen the statistical capacity of institutes in the wider statistical ecosystem and supported the proposal for an in-depth analysis of targeted statistical  / capacity development programmes, underlying methodologies, coordination and modes of delivery of capacity development activities, including hybrid modalities and dissemination of materials in all official languages of the United Nations, and to develop a set of recommendations in collaboration with relevant partners, such as those that are part of the Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training. / This project will implement the core foundation of a "Statistical Capacity Development Knowledge Management System" (CD-KMS) as a minimum viable product (MVP). This initial, operational system will serve as a centralized information management hub to map, track, and analyze all UNSD capacity development (CD) activities, including projects, workshops, missions, publications, and country requests. By leveraging a knowledge-graph approach, the CD-KMS will replace fragmented spreadsheet- and document-based tracking currently in place. It will provide a comprehensive, relational view of UNSD's CD portfolio, linking activities to participants, NSOs, funding sources (RPTC, XB), strategic goals (e.g., VNRs, SDGs), and outputs (mission reports, training materials). The system will significantly enhance UNSD's internal efficiency in planning, monitoring, and reporting, which in turn will improve the coherence, targeting, and effectiveness of capacity development support provided to Member States.

title: titleâ€¢	Report of 55th session of the UN Statistical Commission (2024), decision 53/109: / o	(h) Supported the efforts of international organizations, regional commissions and statistical training institutes in providing technical assistance, organizing workshops and training and developing compilation tools, and noted the importance of ensuring that resources continue to be made available for this work;  / â€¢	Report of the 52nd session of the UN Statistical Commission (2021), decision 51/110: / o	The Statistical Commission welcomed the report of the Committee of Experts on Environmental-Economic Accounting, welcomed the work done thus far on mainstreaming the SEEA as a statistical framework to support various initiatives, including the SDGs, climate change, the circular economy, the ocean agenda, the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and sustainable tourism, commended current usage of SEEA for country-level reporting on the SDGs, and welcomed the integration of SEEA into SDG indicators 15.9.1 and 12.b.1 / â€¢	Report of the 44th session of the UN Statistical Commission (2013), decision 44/104: / o	(b) Adopted the implementation strategy for the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) Central Framework recommending a flexible and modular approach, and urged the Committee of Experts to agree on a medium-term programme of work for the implementation of SEEA, including advancing the issues on the SEEA Central Framework research agenda and the development of a core set of tables and accounts, in order to develop coordination mechanisms among the relevant international and regional agencies for effective management of the programme and to actively seek funding to support the implementation activities;
summary: The System of Environmental Economic Accounting (SEEA) provides the internationally agreed statistical framework for measuring the relationship between the environment and the economy. It is comprised of two complimentary international statistical standards: the SEEA Central Framework (SEEA CF) and the SEEA Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA). The SEEA can be flexibly implemented by countries prioritizing accounts based on availability of information and policy priorities. The accounts are designed to respond to data needs for multiple policy initiatives including global initiatives on sustainable development goals (SDGs), on mitigating and adapting to climate change, disaster related statistics and on measuring the contribution of the environment to well-being. The accounts are also a necessary input to the compilation of headline indicators such as net domestic product as part of the recently adopted 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA). / In Asia, good progress has been made in the compilation of SEEA accounts with many countries regularly compiling SEEA CF accounts. National statistical offices (NSOs) of countries in the region continue to express strong interest in compiling SEEA accounts, including taking steps towards compiling asset accounts which are relevant for informing the relationship between the economy and the environment. With the recent adoption of the 2025 SNA which has expanded its asset boundary to include several natural resources assets of the SEEA CF, demands for environmental asset accounts will increase as the SEEA CF can provide input data for the compilation of the 2025 SNA. More broadly, there is a need to strengthen the capacities of NSOs to produce and disseminate SEEA accounts to better meet the needs of users for high quality integrated data on the contribution of the environment to the economy and the impact of the economy on the environment.

title: titleThe mandate for the proposed activity comes from the resolution adopted by the 56th session of the United Nations Statistical Commission (to be adopted by Economic and Social Council later in 2025) on the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme as well as decision 56/102 of the Statistical Commission. Both the resolution and the decision recognize censuses as key for formulating, implementing, and monitoring inclusive socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability policies, and as a vital source of disaggregated data for tracking the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, including assessments by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location, and other characteristics. As part of the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme, which includes several inter-related objectives and activities, UNSD is mandated to develop international statistical standards, methods, and guidelines to facilitate the conduct of population and housing censuses, and to provide technical assistance for building national capacity in planning and conducting censuses.
summary: The request is for a capacity building workshop to prepare census managers in Anglophone African countries to successfully plan their 2030 round censuses and to effectively implement the Revision 4 of the United Nations Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (P&R Rev.4), endorsed by the 56th session of the Statistical Commission in March 2025. The primary objectives of the workshop include fostering a shared understanding of the updated global standards contained in the P&R Rev.4, enhancing participants' technical proficiencies in applying the revised recommendations (including areas like geospatial data, administrative records, new core topics, contingency planning, quality assurance, and communication), facilitating the exchange of best practices and collaborative problem-solving for anticipated challenges in the upcoming census round, and exploring innovative methodologies and opportunities for future administrative data-based censuses to improve efficiency and quality. / The workshop is jointly organized by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), the African Centre for Statistics at the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Statistics South Africa, and the Office of National Statistics of the United Kingdom (ONS-UK). Participants will include representatives from national statistical offices, such as census managers/coordinators or senior census staff responsible for census planning and implementation, as well as managers/senior technical experts in census operations, such as mapping, data processing, ICT or other relevant areas.

Transfer pricing â€” the pricing of cross-border transactions involving goods, services, or intangibles between related entitiesâ€” has gained increasing global attention due to its significant implications for equitable taxation and sustainable development.  / Developing countries face considerable challenges in this area, including a high risk of profit shifting and limited access to specialized training and resources available to policy makers and tax administrations. title: titleâ€¢	Report of 55th session of the UN Statistical Commission (2024), decision 53/109: / o	(h) Supported the efforts of international organizations, regional commissions and statistical training institutes in providing technical assistance, organizing workshops and training and developing compilation tools, and noted the importance of ensuring that resources continue to be made available for this work;  / â€¢	Report of the 52nd session of the UN Statistical Commission (2021), decision 51/110: / o	The Statistical Commission welcomed the report of the Committee of Experts on Environmental-Economic Accounting, welcomed the work done thus far on mainstreaming the SEEA as a statistical framework to support various initiatives, including the SDGs, climate change, the circular economy, the ocean agenda, the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and sustainable tourism, commended current usage of SEEA for country-level reporting on the SDGs, and welcomed the integration of SEEA into SDG indicators 15.9.1 and 12.b.1 / â€¢	Report of the 44th session of the UN Statistical Commission (2013), decision 44/104: / o	(b) Adopted the implementation strategy for the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) Central Framework recommending a flexible and modular approach, and urged the Committee of Experts to agree on a medium-term programme of work for the implementation of SEEA, including advancing the issues on the SEEA Central Framework research agenda and the development of a core set of tables and accounts, in order to develop coordination mechanisms among the relevant international and regional agencies for effective management of the programme and to actively seek funding to support the implementation activities;
summary: The System of Environmental Economic Accounting (SEEA) provides the internationally agreed statistical framework for measuring the relationship between the environment and the economy. It is comprised of two complimentary international statistical standards: the SEEA Central Framework (SEEA CF) and the SEEA Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA). The SEEA can be flexibly implemented by countries prioritizing accounts based on availability of information and policy priorities. The accounts are designed to respond to data needs for multiple policy initiatives including global initiatives on sustainable development goals (SDGs), on mitigating and adapting to climate change, disaster related statistics and on measuring the contribution of the environment to well-being. The accounts are also a necessary input to the compilation of headline indicators such as net domestic product as part of the recently adopted 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA). / In Asia, good progress has been made in the compilation of SEEA accounts with many countries regularly compiling SEEA CF accounts. National statistical offices (NSOs) of countries in the region continue to express strong interest in compiling SEEA accounts, including taking steps towards compiling asset accounts which are relevant for informing the relationship between the economy and the environment. With the recent adoption of the 2025 SNA which has expanded its asset boundary to include several natural resources assets of the SEEA CF, demands for environmental asset accounts will increase as the SEEA CF can provide input data for the compilation of the 2025 SNA. More broadly, there is a need to strengthen the capacities of NSOs to produce and disseminate SEEA accounts to better meet the needs of users for high quality integrated data on the contribution of the environment to the economy and the impact of the economy on the environment.

title: titleThe mandate for the proposed activity comes from the resolution adopted by the 56th session of the United Nations Statistical Commission (to be adopted by Economic and Social Council later in 2025) on the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme as well as decision 56/102 of the Statistical Commission. Both the resolution and the decision recognize censuses as key for formulating, implementing, and monitoring inclusive socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability policies, and as a vital source of disaggregated data for tracking the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, including assessments by income, sex, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location, and other characteristics. As part of the 2030 World Population and Housing Census Programme, which includes several inter-related objectives and activities, UNSD is mandated to develop international statistical standards, methods, and guidelines to facilitate the conduct of population and housing censuses, and to provide technical assistance for building national capacity in planning and conducting censuses.
summary: The request is for a capacity building workshop to prepare census managers in Anglophone African countries to successfully plan their 2030 round censuses and to effectively implement the Revision 4 of the United Nations Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (P&R Rev.4), endorsed by the 56th session of the Statistical Commission in March 2025. The primary objectives of the workshop include fostering a shared understanding of the updated global standards contained in the P&R Rev.4, enhancing participants' technical proficiencies in applying the revised recommendations (including areas like geospatial data, administrative records, new core topics, contingency planning, quality assurance, and communication), facilitating the exchange of best practices and collaborative problem-solving for anticipated challenges in the upcoming census round, and exploring innovative methodologies and opportunities for future administrative data-based censuses to improve efficiency and quality. / The workshop is jointly organized by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), the African Centre for Statistics at the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Statistics South Africa, and the Office of National Statistics of the United Kingdom (ONS-UK). Participants will include representatives from national statistical offices, such as census managers/coordinators or senior census staff responsible for census planning and implementation, as well as managers/senior technical experts in census operations, such as mapping, data processing, ICT or other relevant areas.

title: titleFSDO will organize two 2-day regional workshops on strengthening the capacity of developing countries to design risk-informed and data driven development cooperation strategies and policies in support of their COVID-19 response and recovery efforts.  The workshops will target national governments of developing countries from Africa and Asia (specifically, Pacific Small Island Developing States (PSIDS)), focusing on those countries that have engaged in the Development Cooperation Forum (DCF) Survey exercise. / The two workshops will employ a peer learning format that brings countries from within the same region together to exchange practical knowledge and experience on strengthening the effectiveness of development cooperation â€“ a core focus of the DCF Survey and FSDO/DESAâ€™s development cooperation workstream. Each workshop will focus on a specific â€œenablerâ€ of effective development cooperation that has been identified by countries within the region as priorities for strengthening â€“ specifically, national development cooperation policies (NDCPs) in Africa and development cooperation information systems (DCIS) in Asia-Pacific.  / The biennial DCF Survey exercise and High-level Meeting of ECOSOCâ€™s Development Cooperation Forum serve as core activities through which developing countriesâ€™ capacity gaps and demand for learning and knowledge exchange are communicated. In addition, demand for peer learning and capacity building activities has been repeatedly expressed by government representatives in DCF policy dialogue (e.g., 2021 DCF High-level Meeting of ECOSOC; DCF regional consultations in December 2021).    / In the Outcome document of the 2022 Financing for Development (FfD) Forum, Member States highlighted â€œthe critical role of resilient international development cooperation in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and addressing global crises, as highlighted by the 2021 high-level meeting of the Development Cooperation Forum.â€ Moreover, they committed â€œto support developing countries in strengthening their capacities at the national and local levels to manage and reduce risks, which entails developing institutional capacities for transitioning to resilient and sustainable development systems.â€  / Based on the above mandates, FSDO and on exchanges with 2021/2022 DCF Survey participants from the Africa and Asia-Pacific regions, FSDO plans to offer the two workshops, which will result in improved knowledge and understanding to advance risk-informed development cooperation for long term resilience, as well as strengthen data systems for monitoring and evaluation for effective development cooperation. / Original reference# 4221

summary: Through the work of the Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) it has been re-confirmed that there is an urgent need to support developing countries in creating and better maintaining statistical training programs at national level. This is key for staff at the National Statistical Systems (NSS) to receive core trainings for doing their jobs efficiently, and will make the NSS less dependent on external partners. / GIST has identified that a key first step is to help countries develop a needs assessment tool to understand the training needs of their staff as well as key development area needs from a managerial perspective. In relation to this, there is also a need to provide guidance on how to prioritise among gaps identified as well as to provide template curriculums for courses that are expected to be core in all countries. / GIST members are actively supporting the work, but are in needs of support in coordinating the work, helping it move forward more quickly to respond to countries needs and ultimately help staff in the NSS improve their skills more systematically to increase efficiency of the NSS in providing quality and timely SDG and other statistics to the public.

title: titleFor more information, see https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/events/latin-america-and-caribbean-workshop-assessing-economic-and-fiscal-consequences-population. / This type of regional training workshop was first piloted at UN ESCAP.   Also note that ECLAC (Pop Division) undertook coordination of a project financed by the United Nations Development Account (10th Tranche) on Demographic Transition: Opportunities and Challenges to Achieve the SDGs in Latin America and the Caribbean.   Seminar was held immediately following this training workshop. / Achievement of an inclusive economic development that leaves no one behind requires good investment and good planning. Because achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030 also means ensuring their sustainability beyond 2030, training in the use of long-run population, economic, and fiscal forecasts is an important component of capacity development as envisioned by Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing.  /   / In this context, the Population Division of DESA and ECLAC organized the Latin American and Caribbean Workshop Assessing the Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Population Ageing, held at ECLAC in Santiago from 9 to 11 September 2019.  /   / While population ageing will be one of the most important forces shaping the outcome of social and economic policy in the coming decades in the Latin America and Caribbean region, it is not always explicitly included in policy discussions. Because its influence is difficult to discern in the short run, a myopic policy focus inevitably results in delays in addressing mounting challenges such as population ageing, climate change, non-communicable disease and environmental degradation.  /   / The Workshop trained participants from national statistical offices, ministries in the planning, economic and social sectors, and research institutions in the use medium- and long-run economic and fiscal forecasts to address the cost, equity, and sustainability of development policies and programmes.

title: titleUNSD has supported Member States in building capacity for SDMX-based reporting and dissemination, especially for MDGs and SDGs. This has led to the development of SDG dissemination platforms in several regions, funded mainly by extra-budgetary sources. RPTC has played a growing role, notably through a successful UNSD-ESCWA initiative in the Arab region. However, many developing countries still require advanced training to fully leverage SDMX.
summary: UNSD is preparing a use case to demonstrate the dissemination of data and the integration of SDG metadata into statistical outputs using the SDMX standard. This initiative focuses on linking SDG metadata with the UNdata mobile applications to enhance the accessibility and usability of statistical information. This use case can be used in workshops and guide participants through the process of extracting SDG data and metadata and integrating them into digital products. To support this, UNSD plans to update both UNdata Android and iOS apps with the latest available 2025 data - these updates will mirror the content of the printed Pocketbook publication. For each included SDG indicator, the apps will feature direct links to corresponding metadata, enabling users to explore definitions, methodologies, and sources seamlessly. / To ensure a fully functional and user-friendly experience, UNSD also plans to address several technical issues identified by both internal and external users in the SDG user interface, APIs and metadata related components of the system. This project not only enhances the visibility and utility of SDG data and metadata but also promotes best practices in data and metadata integration and digital dissemination using SDMX standards. / The proposal covers the contractual services needed to update the UNdata apps and fix some components in the SDG infrastructure, including SDG metadata.

title: titleEndorsed by the United Nations Statistical Commission in June 2008, SDMX is recognized as a preferred standard for data and its related meta-information, and has been approved as an ISO standard (17369:2013). The SDMX initiative was started and is sponsored by eight international organizations (BIS, ECB, Eurostat, OECD, ILO, IMF, UN, and WB). / As coordinator of the Working Group on SDMX for SDG Indicators established by the IAEG-SDGs, UNSD has a responsibility for, and has delivered, capacity building to the Member States in SDMX for SDG monitoring. In different sessions, the UN Statistical Commission has stressed the need for continued technical and financial support for countries to build capacity for the production, monitoring, and reporting of Sustainable Development Goals indicators, including on SDMX and implementing the SDG Geospatial Roadmap. / The workshop is organized jointly by UN ESCWA and UNSD to improve countriesâ€™ skills in mapping, converting, and disseminating SDG data and metadata, raise awareness of the latest developments and promote the implementation of SDMX at the national level. / The workshop is planned to take place in Muscat, Oman, on 10-13 November 2025 (4 days).
summary: At  the 15th session of the ESCWA Statistical Committee, on 16-17 Nov 2022, the member States requested the ESCWA Secretariat to "Support member States in developing strategies to bridge gaps in data flows for sustainable, development indicators, so as to ensure the sustainability and modernization of national reporting platforms, and to exchange statistical data and metadata nationally between components of statistical systems using modern technologies, such as SDMX, to ensure that no one is left behindâ€¦â€ , which follows similar requests made at previous sessions.  / ESCWA and UNSD are addressing these through a series of joint online and in-person training events on SDMX-based dissemination and exchange of SDG data and metadata. The workshop in question is the 8th in the series and will directly contribute to the member Statesâ€™ capacity to exchange and disseminate SDG data and metadata using the global standards and advanced tools, and implementation of SDMX data exchange at the national level.  / The workshop is organized jointly by UN ESCWA and UNSD and is planned to take place in Muscat, Oman, on 10-13 November 2025 (4 days). A pre-workshop meeting will be held on 9 November 2025 to check the venue and final coordination for the event. The Workshop will bring together statisticians and IT specialists from various national statistical offices in the Arab region. / This workshop is a continuation of UNSD and ESCWAâ€™s work to improve and strengthen the SDMX skills of Member States on SDG data reporting and to implement SDMX at the national level. As requested by Member States in the region, the training will cover different SDMX topics and provide hands on exercises with the aim to introduce SDMX tools to enable the automation of data and metadata exchange between entities. It will employ a variety of tools including presentations, hands-on exercises, and the sharing of good practices and challenges by countries through discussions and presentations.

title: titleReport of 55th Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2024), decision 55/109 (h): / o	The Statistical Commission supported the efforts of international organizations, regional commissions and statistical training institutes in providing technical assistance, organizing workshops and training and developing compilation tools, and noted the importance of ensuring that resources continue to be made available for this work  / Report of the 50th Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2019), decision 50/115 (c): / o	The Statistical Commission requested the Committee of Experts to continue its work on mainstreaming the use of SEEA for policy processes, in particular with regards to biodiversity, in view of the adoption of the post-2020 biodiversity agenda, and climate change, circular economy, beyond gross domestic product (GDP) and green growth initiatives / Report of the 42nd Session of the UN Statistical Commission (2011), para. 105 (a), (b), (c): / o	The Statistical Commission welcomed with appreciation the report of the Secretary General on energy statistics (E/CN.3/2011/8) and noted that the work undertaken on the international recommendations for energy statistics illustrates effective cooperation among different agencies, expert groups and countries; adopted the international recommendations for energy statistics; endorsed the main elements of the proposed implementation programme
summary: Climate change is one of the most pressing policy issues around the world, with all countries being vulnerable to its adverse effects. To better mitigate climate change, countries are more and more looking to understand how to use energy more effectively and sustainably. Such an understanding requires countries to have high-quality energy statistics, balances and accounts. Together, energy statistics, balances and accounts can provide governments with the data they need to understand how the energy sector can be made more efficient and sustainable; how the economy can be made more energy efficient; and how changes in energy use can contribute to fewer emissions. ESCWA countries have expressed interest in capacity building on energy statistics and accounts. In addition, according to the 2023 Global Assessment on Environmental-Economic Accounting, Jordan plans to restart compilation of System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) accounts; Morocco and Tunisia have plans to expand its compilation of SEEA accounts; and Somalia has plans to begin compilation of SEEA accounts. / National statistical offices are well placed to produce energy statistics, balances and accounts. Energy statistics and balances can be compiled according to the International Recommendations for Energy Statistics (IRES), and energy accounts can be compiled according to the international statistical standard, the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA). At the same time, there is a need to strengthen the capacity of national statistical offices and other relevant ministries to produce and disseminate energy statistics, balances and accounts to better meet user needs.  / UNSD, in collaboration with ESCWA, SESRIC, IEA and AITRS held the workshop, "Energy Statistics, Balances and Accounts for Informed Energy and Climate Policies" from 10-12 December in Ankara. More than 40 participants from national statistical offices and ministries of energy came together from 10-12 December 2024 in Ankara to build capacity compilation and use of energy statistics, balances and accounts to support the dissemination of high-quality data for energy and climate change policies. The workshop also covered the institutional mechanisms needed to strengthen the institutions producing these statistics and allowed countries to share their experiences.

title: titleBased on the intergovernmental agreed guidance by the UN Forum on Forests (UNFF), the UNFF-Global Forest Financing Facilitation Network (GFFFN) should maintain a list of country requests, provide support whenever capacity and resources become available. The response time by the GFFFN varies based on the availability of fanatical resources, sufficient human resources, and the readiness and internal coordination among different national ministries of countries. Given the limitation of human and financial resources, the average response time to provide GFFFN support is normally more than a year. Upon receipt of this country request, the UNFF Secretariat, consistent with the intergovernmentally agreed guidelines, immediately acknowledged the receipt of the request, and informed them officially of the provision of the GFFFN support once the resources and capacity within the Secretariat become available. At the time of receipt of this request, the UNFF-GFFFN was providing support to a large number of country requests received previously. This request, was, thus placed on the waiting list for support when the capacity at the GFFFN become available upon completion of its ongoing country project.  / In 2020. the COVID-19 pandemic significantly interrupted the GFFFN activities in support of countries, due to travel restrictions and the challenges in conducting national level stakeholder consultations, workshops, etc. The latter was compounded by the reduced human capacity at the UNFFS to support GFFFN activities in the same year. These have resulted in delay in the completion of the ongoing GFFFN activities and the commencement of new GFFFN support to countries in the waiting list. To address these issues and start provision of support, the UNFF-GFFFN is contacting countries in the waiting list to start the work, especially regarding the analytical and feasibility studies in those countries this year (2021).

summary: The Financing for Sustainable Development Office (FSDO) of the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) organized a Regional Workshop on Transfer Pricing in Asia-Pacific, held from 25 to 29 August 2025 in Incheon, Republic of Korea.  / The workshop responded directly to countries' demand for practical tools and training on transfer pricing, aimed at strengthening domestic resource mobilization to support sustainable development. Transfer pricing â€” the pricing of cross-border transactions involving goods, services, or intangibles between related entitiesâ€” has gained increasing global attention due to its significant implications for equitable taxation and sustainable development.  / Developing countries face considerable challenges in this area, including a high risk of profit shifting and limited access to specialized training and resources available to policy makers and tax administrations. The workshop brought together 23 participants (39% female) from 23 countries across the Asia-Pacific region, including least developed countries (LDCs), landlocked developing countries (LLDCs), and small island developing states (SIDS). Participants engaged in hands-on training on transfer pricing principles, using practical case studies to illustrate challenges frequently encountered by tax officials during audits of real-life transfer pricing cases.  / Delivered in English, the workshop contributed to ongoing capacity-building efforts, enhancing the ability of tax officials to effectively address complex international tax issues.

summary: Through the work of the Global Network of Institutions for Statistical Training (GIST) it has been re-confirmed that there is an urgent need to support developing countries in creating and better maintaining statistical training programs at national level. This is key for staff at the National Statistical Systems (NSS) to receive core trainings for doing their jobs efficiently, and will make the NSS less dependent on external partners. / GIST has identified that a key first step is to help countries develop a needs assessment tool to understand the training needs of their staff as well as key development area needs from a managerial perspective. In relation to this, there is also a need to provide guidance on how to prioritise among gaps identified as well as to provide template curriculums for courses that are expected to be core in all countries. / GIST members are actively supporting the work, but are in needs of support in coordinating the work, helping it move forward more quickly to respond to countries needs and ultimately help staff in the NSS improve their skills more systematically to increase efficiency of the NSS in providing quality and timely SDG and other statistics to the public.

title: titlePresentations at the Asia-Pacific Regional Virtual Meeting on Using National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for Intergenerational Policy Advancement, 5-6 October, Jakarta, Indonesia / This virtual meeting sponsored by UNFPA was attended by 155 NTA practitioners, academicians, and government officials from 20 countries in the Asia-Pacific region to discuss the use of evidence from National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for developing forward-looking, intergenerational policies to meet the challenges and opportunities brought about by rapid population change in the region.  I served as panelist on a roundtable discussion on "Improving National Transfer Accounts as a Policy Tool" and also gave a presentation on DESA's Handbook on Population Ageing and Sustainable Development -- which examines issues of intergenerational equity, economic security, fiscal sustainability, and sustainable economic growth. / Presentation at the Asia-Pacific Regional Virtual Meeting on Using National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for Ageing Policy Advancement, 7 October, Jakarta, Indonesia / This virtual meeting sponsored by UNFPA was attended by 60 policy planners and government officials from 20 countries in the Asia-Pacific region to receive feedback on the usefulness of National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for national planning in response to population ageing.  A keynote roundtable comprised of the Thailand Minister of Finance, the Indonesian Vice Minister of Finance, and the Maldives Deputy Minister for National Planning discussed national experiences in implementing population ageing policies.   Following the roundtable,  a staff member of UNFPA and I discussed the UN's past contributions and future support on the use of National Transfer Accounts (NTA) for policy development in the Asia-Pacific region.
summary: UNFPA regional office for Asia and Pacific requests our participation in two regional training workshops on the use of National Transfer Accounts (national accounts disaggregated by age) for evidence-based policy on intergenerational equity and fiscal and economic consequences of population ageing.   Population Division will give two presentations:  (1) the new DESA "Handbook on macroeconomic consequences of population ageing" and (2) UN support for use of National Transfer Accounts for evidence-based policy in Asia and Pacific.   Population Division will also participate in a panel discussion reflecting on the success and failures of National Transfer Accounts as a policy tool.
